#3150. Wall Street Is Ignoring Bristol Myers Squibb's Cash Machine -- and That's an Opportunity for Income Investors

Bristol Myers Squibb has a 4% yield and a 55% payout ratio, which should greatly interest dividend lovers.

Bristol Myers Squibb (BMY -1.57%) traces its history back to the mid-1800s. It is a proven survivor in the highly competitive and innovation-driven pharmaceutical sector. That can't save the company from the normal dynamics of the drug industry, as it works through a period of elevated patent expirations. Investor concerns about patent expirations, however, have turned the company into a dividend machine, yielding 4%. The average pharma stock yields just 1.4%.

Here's why Bristol Myers Squibb could be a buying opportunity for long-term income investors. And it all boils down to the success of the company's "growth portfolio," which is increasingly powering its cash flow.

The pharmaceutical sector follows a normal cycle that every company goes through. To simplify it, a company invests heavily in research and development to identify and secure approval for new drugs; the drugs have strong sales during a period of patent exclusivity; and then sales fall off when the patent expires and generic competition enters the market.

Investors inevitably get worried when patent expirations come up, because it means revenues are going to come under pressure. Right now, Bristol Myers Squibb has some big patent expirations on the horizon, and the stock's price has been relatively weak. However, dividend investors need to put this situation into perspective. The healthcare giant still has a well-covered dividend, highlighted by a 55% trailing 12-month payout ratio in the third quarter.

And revenues from what the company calls its "legacy portfolio" aren't exactly falling off a cliff just yet. In the third quarter, sales from this collection of drugs rose 1%. These drugs represent just over 40% of revenues. The other 60% is the cash flow machine you want to watch.

In the third quarter, the drugs Bristol Myers Squibb puts in its "growth portfolio" generated 12% revenue growth. The list of drugs here includes Opdivo Qvantig, Breyanzi, Reblozyl, Camzyos, and Opdualag. Don't worry too much about the names; just note that it is a fairly long list. This isn't a one-trick pony business. Bristol Myers Squibb is a respected, diversified industry giant with a long and successful history in drug development. And it is already seeing material success on that front.

To be fair, investors aren't exactly ignoring this fact. As the chart below highlights, the stock is up from its lows, and the dividend yield isn't as attractive as it was when it was roughly 6%. Still, the yield is well above the market average and that of the average pharma stock, so there's a very good reason for dividend investors to jump on this cash-flow machine.

The 40% of revenues that fall into the "legacy portfolio" is a problem. And investors need to monitor what's going on with that portfolio. However, it is entirely normal for drugs to become less profitable as generic competition enters the market. So Bristol Myers Squibb is just working through a transition period that it has worked through many times before. If history is any guide, it will survive this period in relative stride.

All of that said, the real issue for Bristol Myers Squibb is the drug Eliquis, which had sales of nearly $4.7 billion in the third quarter. It accounts for most of the company's $5.4 billion of "legacy portfolio" revenues. It will be a big hit when this drug loses patent protection, and there's a lot riding on finding a replacement.

But the "growth portfolio", which generates revenues of $7.6 billion, includes a dozen drugs, and revenue growth across the group has been strong. If you recognize the cash flow machine that's building in this portfolio, you might find Bristol Myers Squibb and its above-average yield an attractive addition to your passive income portfolio.

#3146. Biotech stocks are surging. How investors can play the new drug innovation boom

Moderna gave investors a scare as its stock plunged on Thursday. But it's still one of the hottest biotechs this year. And it's hardly alone – the sector is on a roll and looks poised for more gains.

The iShares Biotechnology ETF (IBB) is up 24% through October 23, building on a 28% gain in 2025. Two dozen of the ETF's 233 holdings have more than doubled year-to-date. Moderna leads the pack with a 587% surge — even after an 18% decline following a leak of clinical data for its cancer vaccine (which was actually positive).

Analysts say a new biotech cycle is underway, fueled by clinical trial results, M&A activity, and promising technologies such as genomics, mRNA — and AI.

"We're in the midst of a powerful innovation cycle," said John Hall, portfolio manager of the T. Rowe Price Biotechnology ETF. "What's super exciting is we're seeing newer modalities start to make it to market." Companies "understand the disease biology better," he adds, and that could ultimately lead to more novel drugs making it to market.

Investors are excited about technologies like mRNA and genomics, along with a steady stream of new drug approvals. The FDA approved about a dozen novel biologic drugs in 2025, out of 46 approvals in total. Roughly 66 novel drugs are in the pipeline for FDA approval, including potential blockbusters like Moderna and Merck's cancer drug for melanoma, and a next-generation obesity drug from Eli Lilly.

Analysts say AI could also lead to more approvals as companies deploy the software to speed up drug development.

"Biotech is a phenomenal application for artificial intelligence and machine learning," says Piper Sandler analyst Ted Tenthoff. "You can set up exciting predictive models that, frankly, can do things that we've never been able to do in the space in terms of novel drug discovery."

Granted, the industry is recovering from a fallow period. The sector's last strong performance was during the Covid era when ultra-low interest rates encouraged investment in early-stage drug developers, and mRNA vaccines fueled a revenue surge for companies like Moderna, Pfizer and Biontech.

The sector then went cold as many early-stage companies fizzled. Demand for Covid vaccines evaporated, and surging interest rates put a chill in IPOs and M&A.

The risks haven't evaporated – this is still a sector whose products take years to develop, resulting in far more failures than successes. But analysts say the outlook is healthier now. While that's reflected in strong performance and richer valuations, there's still good reason to invest.

Recent clinical trial results are stoking excitement that novel drugs in the works could tackle some of the toughest problems in medicine.

Moderna and Merck's melanoma drug, for instance, uses mRNA to trigger an immune response in patients, targeting tumors that have been surgically removed and genetically analyzed. It's not a preventive vaccine, but it uses a similar immunology mechanism and showed a 42% reduction in cancer recurrence or death (used in conjunction with Merck's cancer drug Keytruda).

While the Phase 3 results disappointed Wall Street, oncologists say the outcomes were still highly positive. And they see the technology as a potential game changer, ushering in an era of personalized treatments for cancers. Moderna and Merck have said they aim to submit the drug for FDA approval and get it launched in 2027.

Inflammation treatment is another promising area. AstraZeneca and Amgen recently released positive Phase 3 results for another use for their drug Tezspire, an injectable approved for nasal polyps and asthma. In clinical trials, it showed that it successfully relieved swallowing symptoms and healed microscopic and visual tissue damage in patients with severe throat inflammation.

Roche, meanwhile, notched a win after the FDA approved its drug Enspryng, a therapy to treat rare inflammatory and autoimmune diseases. It became the first and only at-home injection for adults with thyroid eye disease.

Obesity drugs are also advancing beyond the first generation of GLP-1s. Eli Lilly's retatrutide, a "triple agonist" targeting three different hormone receptors, cleared two more clinical trials over the summer. The drug produced 28%-30% weight loss at the highest doses in the study, Lilly said. The company plans to submit the drug for FDA approval in the first quarter of 2027.

Much of the innovation isn't just happening in drug-making – it's also in areas like gene sequencing, mRNA, and high-tech instruments.

Illumina has more than doubled this year. The DNA and gene sequencing company is seeing accelerating demand for its NovaSeq X high-end sequencing platform. Pharmaceutical companies including Bristol-Myers Squibb, Merck and Kura are working with Illumina to develop precision oncology solutions.

Another big winner is 10x Genomics, up more than 300%. The biotech firm offers its lab instruments to help scientists research cancer, immunology and neuroscience. The company's Atera platform is helping produce data sets to train AI models, a process that helps accelerate personalized therapies.

On the AI front, companies are using the technology for more efficient drug discovery, says Shreefāl Mehta, president of Guidant BioTherapeutics. Using AI, "you can now bring a drug to clinical trials with less capital. More investment is also going into companies that are demonstrating that," he said.

Global AI in drug discovery will grow from a $20 billion market in 2025 to more than $160 billion by 2035, according to forecasts by Towards Health, a research and consulting firm.

One other catalyst for the sector could be M&A. Dealmaking for biopharma hit $134 billion in the first half of 2026, up from $112 billion for all of 2025, notes Jeet Mukherjee, biotech analyst at BTIG. That's a positive signal, indicating more drugs in development are showing clinical promise.

It also helps that Big Pharma has a "patent cliff" ahead. Products representing $180 billion of revenue will lose exclusivity by 2030, according to research firm RTW Institute. Companies with looming expiries "are looking for novel products and innovative products to put into their pipeline," Mehta says.

GLP-1 blockbusters have also left some companies flush with cash for acquisitions. Eli Lilly alone has completed 10 acquisition deals in 2026 worth $25 billion.

ETFs can capture the investing theme, though they aren't all alike. The iShares Biotech ETF is one of the lower cost funds. It tracks a market-cap weighted index of biotech stocks, led by companies like Gilead Sciences, Amgen, Vertex Pharmaceuticals, and Moderna.

The State Street SPDR S&P Biotech ETF holds stocks in equal weight, offering more exposure to small- and mid-cap names. Its top holdings are Moderna, Natera, Twist Bioscience and Halozyme Therapeutics.

Piper Sandler calls Illumina and 10x Genomics the "primary infrastructure plays" in the life science arena, saying their technologies are "driving the next generation of precision medicine."

Piper analyst David Westenberg has a buy rating and $305 target on Illumina, implying 14% gains from recent prices around $267. He has a hold rating on 10X with an $80 target, above recent prices around $70.

Twist Bioscience is another name to consider. The company makes customized synthetic DNA and sells DNA sequencing tools. Twist has partnered with Eli Lilly's AI and machine-learning platform and linked up with Anthropic in August to start testing its AI model, Claude, for protein development.

Twist isn't expected to turn an EPS profit until 2029, according to consensus forecasts. But revenue is expected to go from $572 million in 2027 to $833 million in 2029. Analysts have an average target of $168 on the stock, implying 21% returns from recent prices around $138.

In the small-cap space, Piper Sandler's Tenthoff likes Monte Rosa Therapeutics, a pioneer in protein degradation that selectively destroys disease-causing proteins.

The firm has partnered with Novartis to develop a drug for inflammatory conditions and autoimmune diseases. The companies announced a Phase 2 clinical study in September for an autoimmune disease treatment, which has been "triggering milestones to Monte Rosa," Tenthoff said.

Tenthoff has a buy rating and $37 target on the stock, which recently traded around $10.70.

Also in the small-cap arena, BTIG's Mukherjee recommends Faeth Therapeutics.

The biotech is developing a novel two-drug regimen to treat breast cancer and other tumors. The regimen "has the potential to address safety and dosing limitations of another recently approved drug for breast cancer," he says. And it could become "a mainstay of the future breast cancer treatment paradigm and other cancers."

Faeth is a clinical-stage company that has yet to bring a drug to market. Yet the stock is up 93% year-to-date on positive clinical trial results, trading around $18. Mukherjee has a $55 target on it.

Kymera Therapeutics is worth considering too. The company is developing an oral version of the blockbuster drug Dupixent (made and co-developed by Regeneron Pharmaceuticals and Sanofi). Dupixent is an injectable, however, and oral agents "are frequently preferred by patients," Mukherjee says. "The drug has the potential to not only take share from patients taking Dupixent for numerous immunological diseases but also expanding the market to those not taking systemic biologic drugs," he tells CNBC.

Kymera has said it doesn't expect a patent fight over Dupixent because its drug is distinct, not a biosimilar or biologic copy.

T. Rowe's Hall also likes Kymera for its potential "to unlock disease targets that have been classically considered un-druggable." The stock is the second largest holding in T. Rowe's Biotech ETF, accounting for 4.2% of the portfolio.

#3145. Higher Yield vs. Lower Cost: The Critical Differences Between HDV and VIG

VIG emphasizes dividend growers with lower costs, while HDV targets concentrated high-yielding stocks. One delivered 34.6% returns over the past year; the other offers greater stability.

Vanguard Dividend Appreciation ETF (VIG -0.38%) focuses on companies with a history of increasing their payouts, while iShares Core High Dividend ETF (HDV -0.69%) targets a concentrated group of high-yielding domestic equities.

Dividend-focused investors often choose between maximizing current income or betting on long-term capital growth through dividend appreciation. VIG tracks companies that have consistently increased dividends, while HDV selects stocks offering notably high yields today. This comparison examines how their different strategies affect cost, risk, and portfolio composition.

Beta measures price volatility relative to the S&P 500; beta is calculated from monthly returns over the available fund history (up to five years). The 1-yr return represents total return over the trailing 12 months. Dividend yield is the trailing-12-month distribution yield.

The Vanguard fund is the more affordable choice, with a 0.04% expense ratio, which is exactly half the iShares fund's cost. However, investors seeking higher current income may find the iShares fund more appealing, as it offers a trailing yield that is double its peer's distribution.

Vanguard Dividend Appreciation ETF holds 333 positions and emphasizes growth-oriented sectors. Its largest holdings include Microsoft (MSFT -0.99%) at 4.90%, Apple (AAPL -0.52%) at 4.89%, and Broadcom (AVGO +0.74%) at 4.30%. The portfolio leans heavily toward Technology at 27%, Financial Services at 21%, and Healthcare at 19%. The fund was launched in 2006. Vanguard Dividend Appreciation ETF has paid $3.65 per share over the trailing 12 months, which, on its recent ~$248.24 share price, works out to a 1.5% yield.

iShares Core High Dividend ETF maintains a tighter portfolio of 74 holdings, focusing on stability and current income. Its largest positions include Exxonmobil (XOM +0.34%) at 9.61%, Chevron (CVX -0.15%) at 7.26%, and Abbvie (ABBV +1.06%) at 6.80%. This concentrated mix is heavy on Consumer Staples (27%) and Energy (25%), with Healthcare contributing 13%. The fund was launched in 2011. iShares Core High Dividend ETF has paid $0.96 per share over the trailing 12 months, which, on its recent ~$30.99 share price, works out to a 3.1% yield.

For more guidance on ETF investing, check out the full guide at this link.

When comparing the Vanguard Dividend Appreciation ETF (VIG) and the iShares Core High Dividend ETF (HDV), investors should consider several key factors. Let's see what they tell us about each fund.

First, we should examine each fund's strategy. VIG targets U.S. stocks with at least 10 years of growing annual dividend payments. HDV, on the other hand, targets top U.S. dividend-paying stocks based on yield. VIG also holds many more stocks, with around 330 names, while HDV holds about 75.

Two other important factors are historical performance and income potential. Since 2021, VIG has generated a total return of 60%, equating to a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 9.8%. HDV, meanwhile, has delivered an 83% total return, with a 12.9% CAGR. As for direct income potential, HDV delivers more. Its dividend yield of 3.1% is more than twice that of VIG's 1.5.%.

One final factor to weigh is cost. Here, both funds are quite affordable. VIG has the lower annual expense ratio, though, at 0.04%, while HDV's 0.08% is slightly higher.In summary, VIG and HDV both hold dividend stocks, yet they differ in many key respects. HDV delivers higher absolute income and has also generated superior total returns in recent years. As such, many income-oriented investors will favor HDV. That said, VIG could still appeal to extremely cost-conscious investors, given its lower expense ratio.

Jake Lerch has positions in ExxonMobil. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends AbbVie, Apple, Broadcom, Chevron, Microsoft, and Vanguard Dividend Appreciation ETF. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

#3144. Linux Mint 27 arrives next month, and I like it already: New features and other upgrades to expect

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Linux

It starts with a surprise version number: Linux Mint 27 instead of 24. But the next release brings far more changes than that.

Linux Mint, my favorite Linux desktop distribution, is ready for a fresh start.

Its lead developer, Clement “Clem” Lefebvre, announced earlier this year that the team behind it was considering slowing Mint’s release cadence because the old twice-a-year release cycle was time-consuming and constrained their ability to make major changes. So it is that the next release, Linux Mint 27, will appear in your Christmas stocking.

Also: 5 premium Linux distros absolutely worth paying for in 2026

The developers officially changed the designation on Oct. 13th when Mint changed both its release cadence and its numbering. Clem’s happy about the change: it “was a tough decision to make, but we’re really starting to see it pay off. We’re taking on projects and implementing changes which would previously have been considered too large or ambitious.”

The new Mint will use Ubuntu 26.04 Long Term Support (LTS) as its base. As before, it will offer Cinnamon, Xfce, and MATE desktops.

Earlier development snapshots had been labeled Mint 23 “Alfa.” That title was explicitly a placeholder while the team decided its release strategy. Its final name is Adrien. Moving ahead, release numbers will be based on the upcoming year. Clem said, “We’ll no longer use point releases, so the release after that will be 28. You’ll upgrade from 27 to 28 to 29, and so on.” Instead of girls’ names, Mint will use boys’ names for distro titles.

On Halloween, Clem announced the top changes in Mint 27. It starts with Mint bringing hibernation back into its supported desktop configuration through a dedicated Sleep Modes page in its System Administration tool. The page is intended to make enabling and configuring hibernation easier, including addressing its swap-space requirements.

It may not sound like much, but Clem explained it’s actually rather a big deal. “When you close the lid of your laptop, it goes into a sleep mode called “Suspend”. This mode is very useful… but it has a major limitation: It uses power.” People often forget it’s not really off and that your laptop will eventually run out of power. When that happens, “the outcome is worse than a normal shutdown. The session is gone, and the battery is empty.”

Also: Linux Mint vs. RefreshOS: I compared the two best distros for new users

That’s where “Hibernation comes into play. It saves the session to disk and completely shuts down the computer. No power is used. When you reopen the lid, the session is as it was, and so is the battery.”

Another new feature is Superlight. This fresh system-monitoring application replaces the older GNOME System Monitor. It comes with CPU, RAM, swap, GPU, network, disk I/O, temperature, and fan-speed graphs. It also includes per-application and per-process resource views. Battery-equipped systems also get charge and power-flow history.

Its storage analysis is particularly interesting: it can break down disk usage into files and folders, Steam games, and Flatpak applications. That brings several common troubleshooting tasks — “What’s using the CPU?” and “Where did my disk space go?” — into one interface. I’ve been checking it out on a Mint virtual machine (VM), and I like it already.

The Nemo file manager is getting a media preview pane, toggled with F7 or a status-bar button. It supports pictures, audio, and video, and displays associated information — for photographs, that can include the capture date and camera model. I like this feature a lot. I’ve always done a lot of work from file managers going all the way back to the classic Norton Commander and its Linux successor, Midnight Commander.

I’ve said it before, I’ll say it again. You don’t need to ever touch a Linux shell via a terminal to use Mint. But if, like me, you’re an old-school Linux user and you like using the terminal, Velocitty, Mint’s new terminal application, looks interesting. Its announced features include:

The point is to make recurring projects and SSH sessions easier to find and reopen. If you like other terminal programs, my latest fave is the Rust-based WexTerm; you don’t have to use Velocitty.

Unfold is a new archive manager for viewing, creating, and extracting archives. It uses 7-Zip and 7zip-RAR and supports the encryption formats those backends handle, including password-protected archives. Its design goal is simplicity rather than a sprawling feature set.

The new Mint uses Ubuntu 26.04 LTS as its foundation. Mint is also moving from Ubiquity to the Linux Mint Debian Edition live installer for installing the operating system. This fresh installer comes with support for OEM bulk-produced installations, installation on both BIOS and EFI PCs, support for Secure Boot, and LVM/LUKS configurations.

Also: Linux Mint vs. Zorin OS: I’ve tried both Windows alternatives, and here’s my winner

For the Linux kernel, Mint 27 will use version 7.0. Which one exactly? Good question. We’ll see closer to Christmas.

Wayland compatibility remains the goal, but X11 isn’t disappearing. As Clem said in June, “In an ideal scenario, we manage to make Wayland work just as well as X11.” But they’re not there yet.

The central change is a cleanup of existing code. Mint’s longer cycle gives developers room to overhaul several parts of the desktop together, rather than squeezing individual improvements into six-month windows. As Clem put it in the September newsletter, “I don’t think I’ve ever seen so many changes and new features implemented for a single release.”

What that means for you and me will be better laptop power management, more capable built-in utilities, and a more complete collection of everyday desktop applications. For example, I expect the updated Mint will ship with GIMP 3.2.2 as its default photo editor, instead of Mint 22.3’s years-old GIMP 2.10.

#3143. Bluetooth 7 Speeds Are Set to Quadruple in 2027, Especially for Audio

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

The Bluetooth Group has announced a new standard. Here's how it works and when you can expect to benefit from it.

Senior Editor / Home Security and Smart Home

Senior Editor / Home Security and Smart Home

Wireless tech is about to get a whole lot snappier. On Thursday, the Bluetooth Special Interest Group, the trade association that oversees Bluetooth, officially unveiled Bluetooth High Data Throughput, a flagship upgrade set to arrive as part of the Bluetooth Core 7.0 standard. The revision supercharges Bluetooth Low Energy by pushing maximum bit rates to 7.5Mbps, effectively quadrupling the throughput of the existing LE 2M technology. Compatible devices are slated to hit store shelves starting in 2027.

That’s good news for phone users, tablet havers, laptop groupies, smart speaker stans and more. Bluetooth is still the most popular medium-to-short-range wireless standard for connecting devices. But this is a big rollout, and the changes will start with premium wireless, such as earbuds, with other applications following.

Those other applications could include spatial computing, exchanging AI-related info with local devices, connecting to health wearables and a host of smart home applications, like playing Spotify through an Amazon Echo Studio or dimming a smart bulb.

“In practical terms, a smartwatch could sync hours of sensor-rich training data to a phone in seconds. A smart home product could complete a firmware update with little visible downtime,” Damon Barnes, Director of Technical Marketing at the Bluetooth Special Interest Group, told CNET. “Smart glasses and other AI-enabled devices could exchange more data with a companion device or the cloud. And in audio, the additional capacity can support richer experiences, including high-resolution, lossless, surround, and spatial audio.”

A representative from the Bluetooth Special Interest Group didn’t respond to a request for comment.

The biggest change in this update is a new physical layer for Bluetooth. Layers are like different sections of the Bluetooth protocol, and the physical layer is the bedrock of the standard, the foundational layer involved in transmitting and receiving data signals.

Improvements in the physical layer can have very significant effects on all Bluetooth communications. In this case, new modulation schemes let the physical layer handle data more efficiently and transmit more data at once, which is why the speed increases are so significant.

These improvements also make the new standard more efficient, saving battery life in many applications. So your smart lock may last longer before you need to exchange the AA batteries, earbuds won’t need to go back in the case as fast, and so on.

We know the first flagship devices are expected to appear with the technology in early 2027, but don’t have an exact date.

Barnes also told use that since the update is starting with wireless audio, the first devices to see it will be headphones, earbuds and speakers.

With protocol changes like this, it can take some time for new products to reach the market, and manufacturers may take a long time, even years, to adopt it.

#3139. This Warren Buffett Dividend Stock Is the One I'd Buy With $1,000 in November

Warren Buffett's longtime investment offers a straightforward way to benefit from consumer spending.

A $1,000 investment doesn't need to prove its worth immediately. Indeed, the goal for investors should be to buy a piece of a business that can grow its earnings -- and distributions -- for years, and to hold onto that stake long term. American Express (AXP -1.23%) is one such company. Berkshire Hathaway's (BRKA -0.01%) (BRKB -0.25%) longtime association with American Express might put it on some investors' watch lists, but its economics might be what earns it a place in your portfolio.

First, we need to understand American Express' business model. In a nutshell, the company provides a suite of payment-based services. It issues credit cards and charge cards (which are not the same thing), collects fees and interest from the consumers who use them, collects transaction fees from merchants that process payments on its cards, and offers lending services to borrowers. Overall, its business is solid. Revenue grew 9% year over year in its most recent quarter. Billed business increased by 8%.

American Express attracts an affluent customer base that is generally better able to weather economic downturns. Net card fees (the annual fees paid by cardholders regardless of spending volume) provide the company with a subscription-like recurring revenue stream that can help cushion the company from the impact of temporary consumer-spending slowdowns.

That said, like all lenders, its success depends in part on its ability to keep credit losses down. That means that the risk of a severe economic downturn that could lead to a spike in defaults is always one worth considering.

One reason that Berkshire Hathaway has kept American Express such a large part of its stock portfolio for so long is that the company continues to drive shareholder value. In part, it looks like this:

As you can see, its earnings per share have increased roughly threefold since 2016. Granted, there were a few dips along the way, but for the most part, earnings grew steadily. Similarly, the company's annual dividend payments have also nearly tripled.

However, even with its dividend growing nearly threefold in just 10 years, the dividend yield remains a modest 1.1% at the current share price. That means two things. First, management is prudent. They are ensuring that the company can withstand any credit losses that it may have to write off during an economic downturn. Second, by maintaining a moderate rate of dividend increases, management has left itself ample room to raise the dividend further and drive additional shareholder value if economic conditions improve.

The overall case for owning American Express stock is pretty straightforward: It's an iconic brand with a loyal, affluent customer base. Moreover, steady earnings and dividend growth make it a strong building block for a long-term portfolio. Finally, a $1,000 initial investment is a nice middle ground between making a stock a core investment and a symbolic one.

Now we must turn to valuation. Currently, American Express shares trade at a price-to-earnings (P/E) multiple of 18.4. That's just below its 10-year average P/E of 19.5. What's more, it's well below the S&P 500 average multiple of around 25.9. All in all, the stock is affordable, but it's not the cheapest equity you'll find on Wall Street.

As for risks, they are what you might expect for a financial stock. A recession is the main one. Economic downturns often result in slower consumer spending and a rise in unpaid bills -- both of which would dent American Express' bottom line.

In conclusion, American Express is my pick for a Buffett dividend stock to recommend investors buy this month. Its consistent revenue and earnings growth, coupled with rising dividend payments and an affordable valuation, mean it ticks all the core boxes for a Berkshire stock: It's an ideal investment to buy when you're ready to let compound growth and steady dividend reinvestment work over long-term horizons rather than chasing quick gains.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Here are three AI product drops you might've missed this week.

Every week is a busy week in the artificial intelligence industry, and this week is no exception. As voters expressed serious concerns about AI and data centers at the ballot box, OpenAI and Anthropic — makers of ChatGPT and Claude, respectively — each dropped new updates to make their chatbots a little more capable.

All these changes come amid rapidly changing government and financial environments. The midterm elections, in which Democrats handily beat Republican candidates across the country, showed that anti-AI and anti-Big Tech campaigns resonated with voters. Tech critics told CNET this week that there is a clear desire for government officials at every level to change how they interact with technology companies — to keep their campaign promises. The election results are also shaking up Wall Street, as investors’ fears about AI’s long-term financial viability grow.

Smaller updates like these are helpful for everyday AI users, and there’s a benefit for AI companies, too. They can prove they’re competitive in a market that is losing confidence in AI. Here are the three biggest AI updates to ChatGPT and Claude.

Gone are the days when every new AI tool got an immediate general release — and that’s probably for the best. Now, when a major AI lab has a new frontier AI model, it slow-rolls its access, and it starts with cybersecurity defenders. That’s exactly what OpenAI did with its newest model variant, GPT-6 Cyber.

Introducing GPT‑6 Cyber: a major advance in security research that pairs stronger capabilities with better model alignment.The model powered the Linux kernel research we announced yesterday, and security teams at companies like Mozilla, Palo Alto Networks, Calif, and… pic.twitter.com/34uAeNnhwP

GPT-6 Cyber is a version of OpenAI’s newest flagship model that’s specifically made for security research and work. OpenAI says it’s best at finding vulnerabilities and staying in its secure container. Those two things matter a lot. Earlier this fall, an OpenAI model was partially responsible for helping researchers identify a major vulnerability in PHP, a programming language that’s used in the majority of websites. And any improvements to keep AI secure are necessary. We saw many instances this summer of AI agents breaking out of their testing environments and making cybersecurity experts fear future autonomous hacks.

You won’t be able to use GPT-6 Cyber unless you’re a cybersecurity expert who’s part of OpenAI’s Daybreak program. Cisco and Mozilla teams are already using the model, according to OpenAI.

OpenAI also added a minor model update to its AI image model, called ChatGPT Images 2.6. The biggest improvement is its speed; OpenAI says the new model is 50% faster than before. That matters for AI enthusiasts who are generating multiple variations of a prompt. The new model also lets you animate your AI images into short GIFs. It’s available globally now for all ChatGPT users.

This isn’t the return of the long-dead Sora AI video model, but it is a sign that OpenAI isn’t giving up on the creative AI space entirely. Anthropic, by comparison, has never had a traditional AI image or video generator and opted for a design tool that’s better suited for mocking up websites and apps.

Anthropic is teaming up with fintech platform Plaid to help you bring your financial information into its Claude chatbot.

Both companies say they have strong security measures in place to keep your information safe. But CNET always recommends a cautious approach when it comes to sharing your financial information (or any sensitive information) with an AI product.

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, CNET’s parent company, in 2025 filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

#3137. 3 ways Bluetooth 7 upgrades your devices beyond lossless audio

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Bluetooth Core 7.0 could make your smart home devices easier to set up, for one. Here's what we know about the new core specification.

Bluetooth Core 7.0 is here, and each new specification from the Bluetooth Special Interest Group (SIG) offers a glimpse of what we can expect from our devices in the future. The major feature incorporated into the new core standard is High Data Throughput (HDT), which can enable lossless wireless audio and improved multi-channel spatial audio on more Bluetooth devices.

Also: Apple has a Bluetooth problem, and Android is taking advantage

Bluetooth Core 7.0’s standout feature is that it can achieve wireless lossless audio. However, the improvements to the Bluetooth stack architecture — particularly, expanding the Bluetooth spectrum — allow for faster data transfer, improved energy efficiency, more resilient connections, and create more room for devices and their data-intensive applications.

HDT means good news for audiophiles, smart home enthusiasts, VR/XR fans, wellness wearable aficionados, AI companion devotees, and much more. I explained applications of HDT in a wireless audio context earlier this year. Now that it’s officially adopted, here’s what you can expect.

A major milestone in Bluetooth Core 7.0 is the ability to stream lossless audio over a wireless connection. Bluetooth is lossy, requiring data compression that diminishes audio quality. HDT’s faster data transfer and greater wireless data capacity enable it to handle the massive volume of data required to achieve lossless quality.

Also: Your Bose headphones are getting a major Bluetooth upgrade – what to expect

Audiophiles typically avoid wireless headphones for intensive listening due to the necessary data compression, opting for wired headphones that can accommodate larger lossless files. Bluetooth’s innovation here is widely regarded as a major leap in wireless technology.

HDT also promises to standardize spatial audio, with expanded data transfers allowing for multi-channel audio setups. Standardizing this form of audio transmission could mean consumers can expect more affordable brands and products to adopt this premium feature.

Every consumer-friendly feature possible within Bluetooth Core 7.0 can be traced back to its ability to accommodate more devices and their ever-expanding data needs. According to a Bluetooth blog post, Bluetooth HDT delivers nearly four times the previous maximum Bluetooth throughput.

Data throughput is the amount of data received, transmitted, and processed over the Bluetooth network. With nearly four times the processing power, HDT can move more data, faster. HDT increases Bluetooth’s maximum supported bitrate to 7.5 Mbps, up from the current 2 Mbps.

Also: Beware of Bluetooth sniffers: How your favorite gadgets could be exposing your data

The result is shorter download times for a device’s firmware update, faster device location when Find My Device is activated, or faster transfer of a large photo album via Android’s QuickShare or Apple’s AirDrop.

In the same blog post, Øyvind Strøm, executive vice president of the short-range business unit at Nordic Semiconductor, gives examples of a smartwatch syncing hours’ worth of workout data to your phone in seconds, or a pair of headphones, a smart speaker, or a security camera that can download a firmware update with nearly zero interruption to the user experience.

In a smart home context, Bluetooth Low Energy (LE) is the wireless technology that works in the background, connecting your devices. Bluetooth LE is the baseline technology for quick device discovery and connection. The most recent example of this is Apple’s HomeView, which uses Bluetooth LE to discover a nearby, trusted iPhone to unlock that user’s personalized home hub display.

The less you feel its presence through lags, wait times, and dropouts, the better it’s working. HDT’s goal is to make Bluetooth connectivity frictionless, which is especially valuable when your smart lights, shades, speakers, TVs, refrigerators, and more rely on the technology.

Also: Forget Wi-Fi: Apple is betting on Bluetooth with its new home devices

For example, HDT’s improved data throughput could allow doorbells, cameras, and robot vacuums to quickly offload large amounts of data to your smart home hub. It could also enable near-instantaneous setup of a new device onto your smart home network and firmware updates.

Finally, HDT also addressed network stability and reliability, especially in high-traffic areas such as apartment complexes and dense cities, where a busy network can cause delays and backups. Alongside improvements to Wi-Fi and Thread, a truly seamless smart home is on the horizon.

Bluetooth’s Human Interface Device (HID) profile refers to the wireless communication used by peripheral devices, such as mice, keyboards, and game controllers, when connecting to a host device. Smart glasses and controllers connected to XR/VR headsets also use this profile, and their data-intensive computing will benefit greatly from HDT.

Devices using the HID profile can expect HDT to lay the foundation for making cloud gaming more reliable, spatial computing more responsive, and offloading audio/visual data from smart glasses less power-intensive.

Also: Frustrated with your Bluetooth? How multipoint works – and why it sometimes won’t

Additionally, gaming keyboards and mice can expect HDT’s expanded data processing to deliver shorter device communication intervals, reducing latency and lag.

In 2026, we’re starting to see more Bluetooth Core 6.0-equipped devices, with Samsung’s recently announced Galaxy Buds On featuring Bluetooth 6.2. Though Bluetooth’s blog post states that the first application of HDT will be for premium wireless audio, many audio manufacturers are behind, still releasing products with Bluetooth 5.4.

Smartphones, smartwatches, and smart home products tend to move a little faster, with the majority of current Bluetooth Core 6.0 products falling into these categories.

The Bluetooth SIG announced Auracast in 2022, and audio manufacturers are now beginning to adopt this technology more widely. Channel Sounding was released with Bluetooth Core 6.0 in 2024, with some early adopters releasing compatible products this year, including Google’s Pixel Tag and Motorola’s Moto Tag 2; more are expected next year and into 2028. With these adoption cycles in mind, we may be well into the next decade before HDT becomes standard.

From horror to romcoms, these 80s movies were underrated.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

"Top Gun." "Raiders of the Lost Ark." "Ghostbusters." "Back to the Future." "Star Wars: The Empire Strikes Back." Everybody knows — and has probably seen — these '80s movies, but the Me Decade spawned a whole lot more films, many of which you might not have seen. So, let's hop in the DeLorean and go back in time to rediscover some lost classics.

As a child of the 80s, I've picked five movies ranging from horror to comedy, and starring professional wrestlers, a future Batman, and, because it's the 80s, John Cusack.

"Put the glasses on!" Thus starts one of the most epic fight scenes in all of moviedom between Nada (Roddy Piper) and Frank (Keith David). The reason? Nada wants Frank to don the shades and expose him to the fact that aliens have permeated society and are brainwashing earthlings into becoming subservient consumers.

This B-level horror flick directed by John Carpenter has a few other choice lines from Piper, the pro-wrestler-turned-actor, and has even more to say about rampant consumerism and economic inequalities in society. The fight scene itself is so iconic that it was parodied in an episode of "South Park," but that's not the only reason to check out this movie as we head into the holiday shopping season.

John Cusack's fame was still on the rise when he starred in this rom-com as Lane Meyer, a hapless teenager dumped by his girlfriend for the popular ski jock in high school. In typical 80s fashion, he falls for a French exchange student, who helps him get his mojo back — and face his nemesis in a ski race down the mountain.

"Better Off Dead" came out one year after "Sixteen Candles," and four years before "Say Anything," so you can see the young Cusack still perfecting his craft. And, with plenty of quotable moments in this movie, you definitely won't want your two dollars back.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

Watch "Better Off Dead" on Prime Video (buy/rent) now

Catch another star on the rise in this hilarious comedy, which sees pop idol Nick Rivers (Val Kilmer) join a resistance movement in East Germany to free a scientist held captive. Directed by Jim Ambahams, David Zucker, and Jerry Zucker — the geniuses behind "Airplane!" and "The Naked Gun" — this movie is absolutely packed with belly-laughing dialogue and sight gags galore. There's even one scene where everything is filmed backwards.

"Top Secret" is Val Kilmer's first movie credit on IMDB, but you can see early on that he's got the chops for a hugely successful career. He's so baby-faced in this film that it's hard to believe that in just two years, he'd be the chiseled Iceman in "Top Gun."Watch "Top Secret!" on Prime Video (buy/rent) now

"There can be only one." Thus is the premise of "Highlander," which follows an immortal Scot (Christopher Lambert) as he duels others of his kind to become the last one standing. The only way you can kill an immortal? Slicing their head off, which means you get some excellent swordplay throughout this uneven movie.

While Lambert and accent are nominally the star of the film, both Sean Connery and Clancy Brown absolutely dominate their scenes. Brown, especially, is a real treat as the villain Kurgan. As a bonus, the entire soundtrack was scored by Queen, including an incredible rendition of "New York, New York."

While there were several forgettable sequels made — and a remake is in the works with Henry Cavill — do yourself a favor and check out the original.

While its title would have you think that "Evil Dead II" is a sequel, it's more of a remake of the original 1981 film, but with the blood and campiness dialed up to the extreme. A group of college students goes for a little vacation in the woods, but when they play a recording from the Necronomicon (the book of the dead), they unleash an evil terror who tries to kill them all. Their only hope is Ash (Bruce Campbell), who's as quick with a joke as he is with a chainsaw.

The movie, directed by Sam Raimi ("Spider-Man," "Dr. Strange in the Multiverse of Madness"), is carried by Campbell, who really sells the slapstick in sliced-off limbs. If you enjoy this movie, then be sure to check out its sequel "Army of Darkness," which came out in 1992, and is more action than horror — but even funnier.

#3135. Nutex Health (NUTX) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Revenue slipped, but net income surged as compensation costs fell sharply.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Nutex Health Inc. (NUTX -6.75%) reported a decline in total revenue for the first nine months of 2026 compared to the prior year, attributing the change to adjustments in historical collection data and revenue recognition patterns from 2025. Management emphasized a 159% increase in net income for the period, which reflected lower stock-based compensation expenses and a non-cash reduction in contract services. The company reported continued growth in hospital volumes and highlighted a construction pipeline of new facilities scheduled for completion through 2028. Strategic objectives include establishing new provider networks to improve patient care coordination and utilizing federal dispute resolution frameworks to secure fair market-based reimbursement rates.

Operator: Greetings, and welcome to the Nutex Health 2026 third quarter earnings call. [Operator Instructions] Please note, this conference is being recorded. I will now turn the conference over to your host, Vivian Sanders. Please go ahead.

Vivian Sanders: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Nutex Health, Inc.'s Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Call. My name is Vivian Sanders, and I'm happy to serve as your moderator today. We're truly grateful for your participation and your continued interest in our company as we share the highlights of another exceptional quarter. Please note that this call is being recorded for future reference. Joining me this morning are some of our key leaders driving Nutex Health forward. Our Chairman and CEO, Dr. Tom Vo; our Chief Financial Officer, Jon Bates; our President, Dr. Warren Hosseinion; and our Chief Operating Officer, Wes Bamburg.

Together, they'll provide prepared remarks to give you a comprehensive view of our performance, strategies and vision, after which we'll open the floor for your questions. Before I turn things over to Dr. Bo, I'd like to take a moment to address a few important points. Today's discussion may include forward-looking statements, which reflect management's current expectations about our future performance. These statements are based on what we know today, but they're subject to risks, uncertainties and other factors that could cause our actual results to differ from what we'll share.

For a deeper dive into these forward-looking statements and the factors that may influence them, I encourage you to review the press release and Form 10-Q filed earlier this week as well as our various SEC filings. You'll find all the details there. Additionally, we may reference non-GAAP financial measures such as adjusted EBITDA during the call. For those interested in how these metrics reconciled to GAAP standards, please refer to the press release and the Form 10-Q, where we've included that information. With those housekeeping items out of the way, it's my pleasure to hand the call over to Dr. Tom Vo, our Founder and Chief Executive Officer. Dr. Vo, the floor is yours.

Thomas Vo: Thank you, Vivian, and good morning, everyone. I'm pleased to join you today to review Nutex Health's third quarter 2026 results. It was another strong quarter with solid financial results, steady collections, important reimbursement developments and continued growth in hospital volumes. I'll start with our financial and operational performance in the first nine months. For the first three quarters of 2026, total revenue reached $644.9 million, an 11% decrease from $723.6 million for the same period in 2025. Adjusted EBITDA decreased 13% from $243 million to $211.4 million for the first 3 quarters of 2026.

Net income attributable to Nutex increased to $152.9 million for the first 3 quarters of 2026, a 159% increase from $59 million for the same period in 2025. On the volume side, for the first 3 quarters of 2026, our hospitals recorded 154,300 total patient visits, up 10.2% from 140,100 during the same period in 2025. Same hospital growth was 6.3% in the first 9 months of 2026. On the balance sheet, net long-term debt went from $29.2 million at December 31, 2025, to $34.2 million at the end of Q3 2026, still very low relative to our revenue and our expansion pace.

Cash on hand grew to $249.9 million as of September 30, 2026, up from $185.6 million at year-end 2025. Net cash from operating activities was $188.1 million for the first 3 quarters of 2026 compared to $177.7 million in 2025, a 6% increase. Several factors supported our strong performance over the first nine months. Patient volume and acuity continue to rise, supported by renewed internal initiatives and investments. In particular, same hospital growth is significant for us as it means our growth strategy isn't wholly reliant on the opening of new hospitals. Earn-out expenses declined as most legacy facilities under development as of 2022 completed vesting, boosting net income.

Arbitration-related costs decreased following the renegotiation of the HALO MD contract in the second quarter of 2026. Collections remained strong through the third quarter of 2026. The investors may have noticed a decline in both revenue and adjusted EBITDA year-over-year through the first three quarters of 2026. The declines are not necessarily due to weaker collections in 2026, but rather due to an uneven revenue recognition for the first 9 months in 2025, primarily reflected by two factors. First, additional collection data available in 2025 supported higher collection estimates for 2024 services that was recognized in 2025. And second, ineligible charts were included from mid-2024 through the first three quarters of 2025 and adjusted in the fourth quarter of 2025.

We are also starting to see slight differences between collections for hospital versus collections from the physician entity. Physician fee collections are slightly down compared to hospital collection in the third quarter. This may account for some of the decreases in revenue in addition to the factors that I mentioned above. And as a reminder, physician revenue are consolidated in the revenue but eliminated down at the net income level. We are continuing to follow this trend closely. In addition, we are seeing more stabilization of revenue this year compared to this time last year. Lastly, as more internal hospital development commences, the long-term debt would increase accordingly in future quarters. Jon will discuss these details in his report.

Turning to reimbursement. The quarter included several developments that positively reinforce our long-term view of the No Surprises Act, NSA and the independent dispute resolution IDR process. First, as discussed on our last earnings call, federal courts in California, Florida, Pennsylvania, Texas, Connecticut and Georgia issued decisions during the first half of 2026, reinforcing the finality of the IDR award and limiting insurers' ability to challenge arbitration outcomes in courts. In the third quarter, the District Court in Virginia reached a similar conclusion in a case involving Blue Cross Blue Shield of Virginia, bringing the number of states with provider favorable ruling on key IDR issues to at least 7.

We believe these rulings support our view that the laws payment and arbitration requirements should be enforced as written. Second, recent antitrust and consumer protection against insurers by the campus and Michigan attorney generals highlight intensifying regulatory challenges to the activities of insurers, focusing on planned administrative practices, in particular, fiduciary management, hidden fee structures and the lack of transparency of out-of-network pricing mechanism. Among other things, the Kansas lawsuit alleges that insurers inflate the revenue by making below-market initial out-of-network offer in the IDR process, creating an artificial cost savings to maximize the percentage-based administrative fee payable to the insurer, which is tied directly to the suppress payment benchmarks. Third, as disclosed in our August press release, the U.S.

Court of Appeal for the Fifth Circuit issued an unbank decision addressing calculation of the qualifying payment amount or QPA, under the NSA. The court ruled in favor of the Texas Medical Association and other plaintiffs on two of the three issues presented in validating the use of those rates in federal QPA calculations. The QPA is an important benchmark in the IDR process. We have consistently maintained that the use of those rates and other flawed methodologies can distort QPA calculations, contributing to substantial provider underpayments and result in an increase in the volume of IDR disputes. We view the court's decision as a meaningful progress toward a more transparent and balanced reimbursement framework.

Over time, more accurate upfront payments without the use of those rates should reduce the rate for costly and time-consuming arbitration. Fourth, earlier this month, CMS released the results of two latest formal audits, including CareSource of Indiana and the School Employees Retirement System of Ohio. In the CareSource audit, CMS identified deficiencies involving required NSA disclosures, timely delivery of QPA-related information and calculation of the QPA under application regulations. The School Employees Retirement System audit similarly identified deficiencies involving the lack of appropriate QPA disclosures and IDR-related notification requirements. These findings provide further evidence of inconsistent insurer compliance and payment practices, including continued noncompliance with federal guidelines.

We believe stronger oversight and enforcement can help providers receive more timely and accurate reimbursement. Fifth, we are closely monitoring the legislative developments in Washington, D.C., including 2 recent proposals that take materially different approaches to the future of the IDR framework. The Murphy bill will preserve independent arbitration while strengthening enforcement mechanisms and adding penalties for payers that do not timely satisfy IDR awards. We strongly support the Murphy bill and are advocating for its passage. The Pallone bill by contrast, would eliminate the IDR process beginning in 2028 and generally make the payer calculate the QPA the final reimbursement amount for on-network services with limited review of the methodology used to calculate those rates.

We firmly oppose the Pallone proposal. We believe the independent review through the current IDR process is essential when ensuring that reimbursement rates fail to reflect the fair market values as they currently do most of the time. We also expect strong opposition from other provider organizations should the legislation advance. We are also aware of other nonemergency specialties, physician specialties, including anesthesiology, surgery, radiology and medical transportation companies that also use the IDR to seek fair reimbursement. though we are unfamiliar with their outcomes or eligibility. While the Pallone proposal's intended target is the overall IDR process, it is unclear to us which specialty he is targeting.

We suspect that the Pallone bill may aim to limit other nonemergency providers access to the IDR. Federal and state Emtala requirements obligate our hospitals to evaluate every single patient that enters our emergency rooms. We expect similarly insurers to meet their federal obligations under the Prudent Layperson Act by paying fair and reasonable reimbursement to Amtala participating hospitals and emergency medicine providers. We also have no control over all the providers that provide nonemergency services. Nutex's goal is very simple. We seek fair market-based reimbursement for medically necessary care in our communities with comparable payments for comparable services in comparable settings.

Federal laws enacted to achieve this result should be enforced and median in rates calculated accurately without those rates distortions. Turning to growth. We remain confident in our hospital development pipeline and the opportunities ahead. For the remainder of 2026, our active development pipeline includes projects in San Antonio, Texas and Jacksonville, Florida, both of which are expected to open in the fourth quarter. Looking ahead, we have 4 additional projects under active construction with expected completion in late 2027 and early 2028. These facilities represent the next phase of our long-term expansion strategy. Operationally, our priorities remain increasing patient volumes, expanding service lines and appropriately growing observation and inpatient care across the network.

We continue to invest in technology, diagnostics, artificial intelligence and differentiated patient service to enhance clinical quality, improve efficiency and scale the Nutex model. As new technologies become available, our hospitals will be able to offer a broader range of care than ever before. Patient satisfaction remains a core strength. As highlighted in recent press release, our hospitals continue to earn recognition for quality and service, reinforcing our position as a trusted provider for physicians, healthcare professionals and their families in the communities we serve. Wes will provide additional report in his report. Bottom line is that we continue to operate a profitable business with strong cash flow and robust internal and external growth.

So with that, I'll turn the call over to our Chief Financial Officer, Jon Bates, for a detailed review of our financial results. Jon?

Jon Bates: Thanks, Tom, and good morning, everybody. And I'm going to provide some additional details on the financials for Nutex Health's third quarter and first nine months of 2026, another solid period where our earnings are strong and our cash flow continues to build as we plan for two future openings later this year, as Tom indicated, and continue to prove out our growth model year-over-year. So Tom provided a little bit of the bigger picture, let me provide a little more of the detail. So starting with the three months ended September 30, '26 compared to the same period in '25.

As you can see, total revenue for Q3 of '26 was $217.6 million compared to $267.8 million for the same period in '25. Hospital division revenue was $209.1 million for the third quarter of '26 compared to $260.2 million in the prior year period. It was a decrease of 19.7%. Revenue at same hospitals, which are hospitals that were opened by December 31, 2024, decreased by 20.1% for the third quarter of '26 compared to the same period in '25.

But the main reason, so everyone is aware for the revenue decrease period-over-period was due to the larger positive increase in revenue in the 2025 period as the IDR process began showing stronger realization of revenue in the first 9 months of 2025 with us experience the early success with the IDR process. And we discussed some of this in the quarter call, but it's a very similar discussion here.

And if you recall, the revenue per visit, which does include both ER and inpatient services back during the third quarter of 2025 was approximately $5,600 a visit, while cumulative revenue per visit from when we started the IDR process back in July of '24, carrying that through the end of '25 was closer to $4,200, which is more in line with what we have continued to see since then as we came into 2026. So revenue per visit in the Q3 of 2025, again, was positively impacted by adjustments to our collection percentage.

If you recall, it was closer to 65% at the end of December 31, 2024, which is based on what we knew at that point and increased pretty incrementally to 80% by the end of the third quarter of September of 2025. And this positive adjustment was a result of additional historical collection history that we saw realized through those first three quarters of 2025. And as historical collection percentage leveled out to the current average of just over about 80% by the end of 2025, the revenue per visit reflected has been much more consistent from then through 2026.

This helps explain why current revenue per visit is more in line with the historical average measured from the start of the IDR process. And so if there are no significant fluctuations in our collection percentages and other key metrics used to record revenue moving forward, we would expect the revenue visit metric to remain within this similar range. So just regarding the arbitration-related revenue, of the company billable visits, similar to what we discussed in the second quarter, approximately 50% to 60% are submitted through the IDR process, with 40% to 50% of all billable visits resulting in an award determination.

And when an award determination is made, Nutex has prevailed in over 80% of those terminations over the last nine months and collects on average over 80% of the award amounts as calculated on awards from inception through March of 2026. So hospital division visits did increase by 18.1% or 8,390 visits to 54,622 visits in Q3 of '26 versus 46,232 visits in the same period in '25, with same hospital visits growing at 12.4% over the same period. Talking about the Population Health division, revenue grew approximately 13% to $8.5 million for Q3 of 2026 versus $7.6 million for the same period in 2025. And Warren will talk a little bit more about that in a minute.

Total facility level operating costs and expenses represented 53.3% or $116.1 million of the total revenue for Q3 '26 versus the 42.2% or $112.9 million for the same period in '25. With regard to stock compensation expense for the three months ended September 30, 2026, it was $7.4 million compared to a $13.2 million expense for the same period in 2025, which was a $5.8 million decrease in quarter 3 of '26. Currently, there are only two facilities that are part of this major expense that goes into this line item with both of them completing their earn-out period in the fourth quarter of 2026.

The gross profit for the three months ended September 30, 2026, is $101.5 million or 46.7% of total revenue as compared to $54.9 million or 57.8% of total revenue in the same period in 2025, an 11.2% decrease for the three months ended September 30 of '26 versus '25. From a corporate and other cost perspective, the general and administrative expenses as a percentage of total revenue for the three months ended September of '26 was 7.8% or $17 million compared to 4.2% or $11.3 million for the same period in '25.

Operating income for the three months ended September of '26 was $77.1 million compared to $130 million for the same period in '25, which is a decrease of $53.3 million. Net income attributable to Nutex was $40.2 million for 2026 period versus $55.4 million for 2025, a decrease of $15.2 million. Adjusted EBITDA attributable to Nutex went from $98.5 million in Q3 of '25 to $63.9 million in Q3 of '26. Now we'll move on to the nine months ended September '26 compared to the same period in '25. Total revenue for the first nine months of '26 was $64.9 million compared to $123.6 million for the same period in '25.

Hospital division revenue was $618.5 million for the first nine months of '26 compared to $700.5 million in the prior period, a decrease of 11.7%. And same-hospital revenue decreased corresponding 11.2% for the first nine months of '26 compared to the same period in '25. As discussed during the third kind of third quarter explanation for the decrease in revenue for this period, the main reason for the change period-over-period was due to the larger positive increase in revenue in the 2025 period as the IDR process began, showing stronger realization of revenue in the first nine months of '25 with us experiencing early success with the IDR process.

On the hospital visits for the nine-month period increased by 10.2% or 14,252 visits to 254,326 visits for the first nine months of 2026 versus 140,074 visits in the same period in '25, with same hospital visits growing at 6.3% over the same period. Regarding Population Health division, revenue grew approximately 14% to $26.3 million for the first nine months of '26 versus $23.1 million for the same period in 2025. Now in addition to the visit growth noted above, facility and corporate costs also showed improvement for the first nine months of 2026 relative to '25.

Total facility level operating costs and expenses decreased $15.1 million during the period, representing 48.1% or $310.3 million of total revenue for the first nine months of '26 versus 45% or $325 million for the same period in 2025. And the main reason for most of the overall increase in this line was due to the contract services decrease during the period, primarily resulting from the reduction in the CMS fee and the impact from the amendment to the HALOMD contract that was signed in the second quarter of 2026 and was discussed back in the second quarter earnings call.

Total stock compensation expense for the nine months ended September 30 was $6.4 million compared to $119.6 million for the same period in 2025, which was $113.2 million decrease in '26. So we finalized one hospital earn-out at March 31, 2026, and as discussed previously, have two more facilities currently in their measurement periods with both of them completing the measurement period in the fourth quarter of 2026. The gross profit for the nine months ended September 30, 2026, was $334.5 million or 51.9% of total revenue as compared to $398.1 million or 55% of total revenue in the same period in '25.

From a corporate and other cost perspective, the general and administrative expenses as a percentage of total revenue for the nine months ended September 30 of '26 was 7.5% or $48.1 million as compared to 4.7% or $33.8 million for the same period in '25. Operating income for the nine months ended September 30 of '26 was $280 million compared to $244.7 million for the same period in '25, an increase of $35.4 million. Net income attributable to Nutex was $152.9 million for 2026 compared to $59 million for 2025, an increase of $93.8 million.

Adjusted EBITDA attributable to Nutex was $211 million for the nine months ended September 30, '26 compared to $243 million for the same period in '25, a decrease of $31.5 million or 13%. Now looking at our balance sheet, and Tom referenced this earlier, at September 30, 2026, it remains extremely strong with total assets at just above $1 billion. And of that, it includes just under $250 million of cash as compared to $918 million in total assets and $185.6 million in cash and cash equivalents as of December 31, 2025. Additionally, accounts receivable, it increased by $36.6 million to $356.1 million in September -- or at September 30, '26 from $319.4 million at the end of 2025.

We had another strong collection quarter, which provides us continued confidence in this increase. Regarding cash flow, net cash from operating activities increased by $10.3 million for the nine months ended September 30, 2026, to $188.1 million as compared to $177.7 million for the same period in 2025. And as Tom alluded to earlier on the liability side, we really don't have much real debt. Our total bank equipment type debt decreased by less than $1 million to about $42.7 million at September 30, '26 from $43.5 million at the end of the year 2025. Again, with the majority of those items being equipment loans at hospitals for such items as MRIs, x-rays, ultrasounds and CT mines.

With all that said, our balance sheet remains very solid, and we provided our company the flexibility to execute on our growth plan in 2026 and beyond. Now on to Warren Hosseinion, our President, for the population health update. Warren?

Warren Hosseinion: Thank you, Jon, and good morning, everyone. It's great to be with you today to discuss how Nutex Health is advancing population health management. In the third quarter of 2026, we continue to make strides in this area. This morning, I would like to again focus on our strategy and our upcoming goals. Let's start with where we are today. Our Population Health Management division now oversees a diverse group of almost 40,000 members across our platform, including a mix of Medicare Advantage, commercial and Medicaid managed care members. We currently have independent physician associations or IPAs in Southern California, Houston, Phoenix and South Florida.

We have also set up two more in Dallas and San Antonio, where we plan on enrolling patients in 2027. Revenue for the division was $26.3 million for the nine months ended September 30, 2026, up from $23.1 million for the same period in 2025. The healthcare industry is undergoing significant transformation. Health care expenditures continue to place substantial pressure on employers, government programs, insurers and patients. At the same time, the population is aging, chronic conditions are becoming increasingly prevalent and the demand for accessible high-quality medical services continues to grow. The traditional fee-for-service model, which generally rewards the volume of services delivered is increasingly being supplemented by value-based care arrangements that emphasize quality, efficiency and patient outcomes.

We believe this transition represents a substantial long-term opportunity for organizations that can successfully manage patient populations, coordinate care and demonstrate measurable improvements in healthcare delivery. We believe our Population Health Management division is strategically positioned to participate in this transformation. Our approach is centered on the integration of physicians, facilities, technology and data analytics. By working collaboratively with providers and other healthcare partners, we seek to improve the coordination of care across the patient journey. Our core strategy revolves around physician networks. Our IPAs are comprised of networks of contracted and credentialed primary care physicians and specialists located around our facilities. Building strong partnerships with local doctors is critical.

By forming these IPAs, we are building awareness of our hospitals among the local community doctors and their patients. We believe that over time, these relationships will not only increase the volume of IPA and non-IPA patients to our hospitals, but also create a web of care that's seamless for patients. Our vision is that our hospitals and IPAs will work hand-in-hand to amplify our reach and effectiveness. We are fostering collaboration, sharing best practices and ensuring every provider is aligned with our patient-first culture. Going forward, our goal is to build one to two new IPAs around our hospitals every year. With that, I'll turn it over to Wes Bamburg, our Chief Operating Officer.

Wesley Bamburg: Thank you, Warren, and good morning, everyone. As Tom and Jon discussed, patient demand remained strong during the third quarter. I'll focus my comments this morning on how our hospitals are supporting that growth through clinical execution, business development and workforce stability. We saw that demand clearly in our patient volumes. Hospital visits increased 18.1% compared to the prior year, while same-hospital visits increased 12.4%. This growth reflects strong demand across our markets and continued execution at both newer and more established facilities. As our facilities mature, we continue to expand the range of care they can provide. We are investing in technology and clinical capabilities from advanced diagnostic imaging and specialty services that improve how we deliver care.

That includes the thoughtful use of AI and automation to support our clinical teams, streamline workflows and help physicians spend more time with patients. Together, these investments broaden the services available in each community, allowing us to serve more patients locally, strengthening continuity of care and appropriately grow observation and inpatient services across the network. The physician relationships that Warren just discussed are also important to this strategy. Stronger alignment with local primary care physicians and specialists can improve care coordination, increase awareness of our hospitals capabilities and help patients receive appropriate care closer to home. We are also leveraging business development more systematically across the organization. Each of our facilities has local business development leadership focused on its markets.

We're offering support through a corporate structure that coordinates strategy and shares best practices. So through community events, outreach, sponsorships, physician engagement and other local initiatives, we are strengthening community relationships and increasing awareness of the services our hospitals provide. On to workforce. Workforce stability remains another important component of our performance. Employee turnover was 9.6% through the first nine months of 2026. Maintaining an experienced workforce supports clinical continuity, operational consistency and our ability to respond as patient volumes increase. This has a direct impact on our patient experience, which remains a key priority for us.

Our hospitals maintained an average Google rating of 4.76 stars during the period, reflecting the daily work of our physicians, nurses and hospital teams to deliver high-quality patient-centered care every day. From an operational perspective, our priorities remain straightforward: align staffing with demand, improve productivity and resource utilization, standardize effective practices that drive volume growth and prepare our infrastructure to support future hospital openings. Overall, the third quarter demonstrated that our existing hospitals can support meaningful volume growth while maintaining workforce stability, patient experience and operating discipline. We remain focused on translating that momentum into consistent execution and sustainable growth across the enterprise. Thank you, everyone, and I'll turn the call back over to Vivian.

Vivian Sanders: Thank you, Wes and team, for those updates. I will now turn it over to our operator, who will begin the Q&A portion of the call.

Jeffrey Cohen: Okay. And then finally for us, could you talk a little bit about the net income to noncontrolling interest? I think we modeled in about $20 million on a quarterly basis. You came in lighter. What would you expect that to look like in the fourth quarter and beyond?

So we're still a long ways away from any of that happening. Obviously, insurance company will do everything they can to maximize their profit. Operator: We'll hear next from Thomas McGovern with Maxim Group.

Thomas McGovern: So we just talked about shifting payer behavior, but I'm curious to understand the shift in provider behavior as well. Do you know that on a systemwide, have they seen higher engagement from providers? Just trying to understand how engagement is trending within IDR.

Jon Bates: Yes, it's a great question. It's early in that process. I think generally, it has slightly increased. But outside of that, I think we need a couple more quarters to sort of watch the process. And as we've talked about before, I mean, it's nice to lower it from $115 to $15, $100 is great, but that's $100. So the question is, is that enough to change people's decision if they feel like they're not being paid purely on the front end. I think in some cases, it does. In other cases, I don't know that it has that much of a difference outside.

But I think the other positives of what the CMS has done is the portal is opening up, so the information being able to go from outside in through it and for the whole process of the IDR, it just becomes more efficient. And so I think in the end, it's going to really help with just the cleanliness of the data going in. I think the timeliness of things happening, I think it will be quicker as well. So I think that might be as much or bigger of a positive from some of those changes that we talked about in the second quarter.

I think we are seeing some of it now, but I think it's going to be another quarter or two until we really see it realize itself, but really good question.

Thomas Vo: Yes. Thomas, remember that there are other factors besides for the CMS fees. Obviously, to Jon's point, CMS has made it much easier for providers to initiate IDR and arbitration.
