#3113. Consumer Staples Showdown: Weighing the Differences Between VDC and RSPS

Vanguard delivered 21.3% returns over one year with lower costs, while Invesco's equal-weighting approach offers higher dividend income at 2.8%.

The Vanguard Consumer Staples ETF (VDC -1.16%) offers broad sector exposure with very low costs, while the Invesco S&P 500 Equal Weight Consumer Staples ETF (RSPS -1.34%) equally weights its holdings to reduce concentration risk.

Both exchange-traded funds provide a defensive anchor for portfolios by targeting non-discretionary goods, yet they differ sharply in construction. One relies on market-capitalization weighting, which can lead to top-heavy positions, whereas the other ensures that every company in the index carries an equal influence regardless of its market value.

Beta measures price volatility relative to the S&P 500; beta is calculated from monthly returns over the available fund history (up to five years). The 1-yr return represents total return over the trailing 12 months. Dividend yield is the trailing-12-month distribution yield.

The Vanguard fund is the more affordable choice for long-term investors with its 0.09% expense ratio. While the Invesco fund is more expensive at 0.4%, it offers a noticeably higher payout for income-focused investors.

The Vanguard Consumer Staples ETF holds 103 positions, providing broad exposure, with 98% of the portfolio concentrated in the consumer defensive sector. Its largest holdings include Walmart Inc (WMT -1.72%) at 13.86%, Costco Wholesale Corp (COST -1.13%) at 12.12%, and Procter & Gamble Co. (PG -1.02%) at 9.90%. It was launched in 2004 and manages its portfolio without specific quirks. Vanguard Consumer Staples ETF has paid $4.88 per share over the trailing 12 months, which, on its recent ~$246.9 share price, works out to a 2% yield.

The Invesco S&P 500 Equal Weight Consumer Staples ETF is more focused, with 34 holdings, and employs an equal-weighting strategy to prevent any single stock from dominating the fund. Its portfolio is 94% consumer defensive, with 3% in both consumer cyclical and basic materials. Its largest positions include Kimberly-Clark Corp (KMB -1.84%) at 5.47%, Kroger Co. (KR -2.49%) at 3.33%, and Walmart at 3.32%. It was launched in 2006. Invesco S&P 500 Equal Weight Consumer Staples ETF has paid $0.89 per share over the trailing 12 months, which, on its recent ~$32.0 share price, works out to a 2.8% yield.

For more guidance on ETF investing, check out the full guide at this link.

When comparing the Vanguard Consumer Staples ETF (VDC) and the Invesco S&P 500 Equal Weight Consumer Staples ETF (RSPS), investors should consider several key factors. Let's see what they tell us about each fund.

First, we should examine each fund's strategy. VDC is a market-weighted fund that includes consumer staples stocks from the large-cap, mid-cap, and small-cap segments. RSPS, on the other hand, is an equal-weighted fund that includes consumer staples stocks from the S&P 500. VDC holds about 100 stocks, while RSPS holds far fewer, around 40 in all.

Two other important factors are historical performance and income potential. Over the last five years, VDC has generated a total return of 45%, equating to a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 7.7%. RSPS, by contrast, has delivered a total return of 14%, with a 2.7% CAGR. Both funds have underperformed the S&P 500 over this period. As for income, RSPS delivers the higher yield, at 2.8% versus only 2% for VDC.

One final factor to weigh is cost. Here, VDC gains an advantage. Its 0.09% annual expense ratio is far lower than RSPS's 0.40%. For context, if a person were to invest $10,000 in both funds, they should expect to pay $9 in annual fees for their VDC shares but $40 for their RSPS shares.In summary, VDC and RSPS both hold consumer staples stocks, but there are important differences in their structures. Many investors will favor VDC given its lower fees and superior historical returns. However, those seeking an equal-weighted approach or higher yields may still consider RSPS.

#3112. Pet Insurance on Your Mind? Buy It Now, Not Later

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

If your pet is young and healthy, the cost of coverage may not seem worth it. But that math can change fast.

Senior Writer & Licensed Insurance Specialist

It feels natural to protect your pet’s health with insurance in the same way you protect your loved ones with health insurance. After all, fur babies are part of the family.

But if you’ve shopped for pet insurance recently, you might have cringed at the cost. Should you really pay hundreds of dollars every year for something you might not use? For some pet parents, the answer is yes, even if their pet is young and healthy. And that’s partly because of how pet insurance handles pre-existing conditions.

A pre-existing condition is any illness or injury that shows symptoms before your pet insurance policy takes effect. Pet insurers usually won’t cover these conditions.

Dr. Rebecca Greenstein, chief veterinarian at Kleinburg Veterinary Hospital and veterinary expert for rover.com, says she’s seeing an increase in claim denials based on pre-existing conditions. “The whole point of insurance is you want broad spectrum coverage for a variety of things,” she says. “By the time they're excluding major organ systems and anything related to that, you may be paying monthly for coverage that doesn't actually help you when you need to go make a claim.”

If you’re considering pet insurance, it’s best to buy a policy before your pet needs it.

Your pet’s pre-existing conditions will determine which treatments and procedures insurers cover down the road.

Say your dog has a history of allergies. If you buy a policy after your four-footed friend has shown symptoms, pet insurers typically won’t pay for allergy shots or other treatments. The exclusion might also apply to related problems like itchiness or ear infections, says Dr. Michael Goldstein, medical director at Billerica Veterinary Hospital and Thrive Pet Healthcare.

He offers the example of a dog who goes to the vet for a hotspot one year and an ear infection the next. If you got pet insurance for your dog between those visits, the insurer might deny your claim because both issues could be caused by underlying allergies.

The best way around this type of scenario is to buy coverage when your pet is young, before any symptoms develop.

» MORE: The best pet insurance for pre-existing conditions

It’s tricky to figure out if pet insurance will actually save you money in the long run. The most common type of plan covers accidents and illness. It costs an average of $836 for dogs and $435 for cats each year, according to the North American Pet Health Insurance Association (NAPHIA). You could pay these premiums for years before an emergency surgery or chronic illness makes its way to your financial doorstep.

It’s impossible to know for sure whether your pet will stay healthy or run up sky-high vet bills. But you can assess the potential value of pet insurance by looking at common chronic conditions that pets develop with age and how much it costs to treat them.

For instance, “cats generally, as younger animals, don't have a lot of problems,” Goldstein says. “But as they get older, there are definitely common issues. Older cats in particular get chronic kidney disease.”

In cats over age 10, the Cornell Feline Health Center estimates that as many as 40% have chronic kidney disease. The annual cost to treat this condition can top $1,200.

Another example is atopic dermatitis from skin allergies, a common ailment affecting as many as 15% of dogs, according to the Cornell Richard P. Riney Canine Health Center. A single vet visit to address these itchy, persistent symptoms can cost $250 or more. And while that’s a fraction of what you might pay for pet insurance, costs of chronic conditions can add up over your pet’s lifetime.

Vet bills can also balloon quickly if chronic conditions require surgery. One example of this is hip dysplasia, a genetic disorder that can cause arthritis and pain in large-breed dogs. Depending on the procedure, you could pay up to $10,000 for hip surgery.

Many pet insurance plans cover treatments for hip dysplasia, including surgical costs, as long as it's not a pre-existing condition. However, some policies have waiting periods of six to 12 months for orthopedic issues like hip dysplasia. If symptoms develop during that waiting period, the condition will be considered pre-existing. That’s another argument for buying your pet’s coverage earlier rather than later.

Most importantly, having insurance means you can choose the best treatment for your pet no matter the cost. “It's really tragic when it's a life and death decision that is needed and it’s based on someone's financial constraints,” Greenstein says. “What is best and what's affordable often are not on the same side of the spectrum.”

One option to keep pet insurance affordable is to buy an accident-only plan. This type of coverage is usually much cheaper, costing about $190 annually for dogs and $112 for cats, according to NAPHIA. These plans cover injuries resulting from accidents, which include not just wounds and broken bones but also objects or toxins your pet might swallow.

However, an accident-only plan won’t help with some of the most common vet expenses. Illnesses, not injuries, are behind most claims submitted to pet insurer Lemonade, the company said in an email. In the past year, more than 60% of Lemonade's pet insurance claims stemmed from illnesses. That’s twice as many as the next-largest claim category, which was preventive care. A similar trend can be found in data from Nationwide, where chronic diseases make up a clear majority of pet insurance claims submitted to the company in 2025.

If you opt for an accident-only plan or no coverage at all, it’s still smart to set aside some savings for those inevitable pet emergencies and illnesses. This pool of funds can keep you from having to make difficult decisions about your pet’s care based solely on the cost of treatment.

#3111. Investors are doing just as well this year by shunning AI. How to invest if the tech trade keeps fizzling

A version of the S&P 500 without AI briefly pulled ahead of the traditional index this year and is now neck-and-neck as investors rotate into other areas of the market.

A proprietary Goldman Sachs index tracking the S&P 500 without stocks classified as "AI enablers" was up 12.4% through Oct. 22, edging ahead of the standard S&P 500's 12% gain. The Goldman index is now neck-and-neck with the S&P 500 as tech rallied in Monday trading.

Tech and AI-related companies make up about 45% of the S&P 500. That heavy weighting has helped power the index for years, but it's turned into a liability lately; the S&P 500 tech sector is down about 7% this month while other sectors have held up.

Investors have soured on debt and equity issued by companies like CoreWeave and Oracle. Shares of Meta Platforms sank almost 7% Thursday after it outlined more plans to spend heavily on capex and issue additional shares.

Companies supplying power and equipment for the buildout have been hit hard — names like GE Vernova, Bloom Energy, Vistra and Quanta Services all suffered steep declines during the recent selloff.

Goldman, which launched the measure earlier this year with S&P, uses the S&P 500 as its starting universe and excludes companies perceived to be enablers of AI before applying S&P 500 Index weighting methodology to the remaining universe of companies.

The ex-AI index lagged the S&P 500 for most of the year as investors continued to favor chipmakers, cloud-computing companies and other firms benefiting from heavy AI spending. However, that advantage has been narrowing and it disappeared last week.

Meanwhile, investors are rotating into defensive areas. ETFs like State Street Consumer Staples Select Sector SPDR ETF, State Street Health Select SPDR ETF and State Street Utilities Select Sector SPDR ETF are up 7% to 10% this month. Energy is ahead 10% too, though that's more related to the war in Iran.

Some analysts recommend sticking with non-AI companies for diversification and protection against more pain in tech. The "AI pendulum has swung back in favor of non-AI exposure over the last two weeks," Oppenheimer technical analyst Ari Wald said in a note on Oct. 24.

Two industries that Oppenheimer favors now are commercial services and insurance. The firm upgraded those industries to overweight last week, recommending Republic Services, Cintas, Verisk Analytics, Broadridge Financial Solutions, MetLife and Arthur J. Gallagher.

Berkshire Hathaway is also capitalizing on the rotation out of tech. Its Class B shares are up 8% this month, though it's still lagging behind the S&P 500 this year.

Berkshire owns a wide swath of operating companies, including insurance giant Geico and Burlington Northern Santa Fe railroad. It also has a $364 billion stock portfolio including companies like Apple, Coca-Cola, Alphabet and Bank of America. That diversification may help Berkshire continue to outperform if the tech sector drags down the S&P 500.

Trivector Research sees potential in "non-tech compounders." Healthcare giant Eli Lilly is one idea. The stock is up 22% on the strength of Lilly's weight-loss drugs. The company has more in the pipeline, including a next-generation obesity drug that Lilly plans to file for FDA approval early in 2027.

Viking Holdings, a cruise operator, is also proving durable. The company said on its August earnings call that 40% of its river capacity and 60% of its ocean capacity was already booked for 2027. "Based on recent events, we've seen our guests have proved to be resilient and are continuing to book 2027 and future seasons," the company told investors.

Viking stock is up 15% this year but it may still have upside. The average Wall Street target is $109, above recent prices around $82. Barclays recently upgraded the cruise operator to overweight with a $102 target, citing the company's "compelling risk/reward."

#3110. American Healthcare REIT: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Relationship-driven sourcing lets American Healthcare REIT buy newer infill senior housing without bidding against rivals in public auctions.

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 6, 2026, American Healthcare REIT (AHR +3.34%) announced an increase to its full-year normalized funds from operations (NFFO) guidance, a cash-flow performance metric for real estate investment trusts. For long-term investors, operational efficiency across senior housing properties is driving compounding cash flows. Three things management said stand out.

In the Senior Housing Operating Portfolio (SHOP), where American Healthcare REIT retains direct operational exposure, revenue per occupied room grew much faster than operating expenses per room. That widening spread expanded operating margins and drove substantially higher same-store net operating income (NOI)--property cash flow after operating costs--across the segment.

Rather than competing in public auctions where asset prices are bid up, management relies on direct relationships with operators to acquire properties. This off-market strategy allows the real estate investment trust (REIT) to buy newer senior housing communities in supply-constrained infill markets without overpaying.

Management reduced net debt relative to earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA), expanding its funding capacity. By match-funding acquisitions through unsettled forward equity sales, the company supports its pipeline while preserving financial flexibility.

Aging demographics provide structural growth tailwinds for senior housing communities. Management relies on proprietary technology tools and regional operator partnerships to turn sector fundamentals into operational execution.

Capital deployment remains focused on disciplined match-funding for acquisitions in high-barrier markets while maintaining low leverage.

#3109. Elon Musk Is Winding Down Cybertruck Production to Build Cybercabs. The Model S and Model X Already Gave Up Their Factory Space to Robots.

The vehicles making room for Tesla's robots sold just a sliver of its cars. But what's the company getting in exchange?

Tesla (TSLA +4.23%) CEO Elon Musk said in a post on X on Friday that the company will wind down Cybertruck production at its Texas factory around the middle of next year. The goal is to make room for more Cybercabs, Tesla's two-seat robotaxi. Musk didn't say if Tesla would build the truck somewhere else.

The Cybertruck isn't the first vehicle to give up its place this year. In January, Musk said Tesla would stop production of the Model S and Model X. The company has since replaced those lines at its Fremont, California, plant with production of its Optimus humanoid robot.

At first glance, this is a big shake-up of Tesla's lineup. Measured by sales, though, it isn't.

Vehicles other than the Model 3 and Model Y (mostly the Model S, Model X, and Cybertruck) made up about 3% of the EV maker's 1.64 million deliveries in 2025.

Measured by factory space, the change is much bigger. And I think the gap between those two measures matters more for the stock than for the car business.

Showing how much room these three vehicles took up, Tesla's installed-capacity table at the end of 2025 rated its Model S and Model X line at 100,000 vehicles a year and its Cybertruck line at over 125,000. Combined, they could build more than 225,000 vehicles yearly, or almost 10% of the more than 2.35 million vehicles Tesla's car plants were rated for.

But Tesla made just 53,900 vehicles outside the Model 3 and Model Y in all of 2025 -- under a quarter of what those lines were built for. And deliveries in this group dropped 40% from 2024, to 50,850.

The slide kept going in 2026. Other-model deliveries fell from 16,130 in the first quarter (probably boosted by final orders for the S and X) to 12,364 in the second quarter and 8,295 in the third. The third-quarter total was down 48% year over year.

The Cybertruck, of course, never got close to filling its line. Tesla doesn't break out sales by model, but Cox Automotive estimated U.S. Cybertruck sales at around 20,000 in 2025, down from about 39,000 in 2024. Musk once said the truck would one day sell 250,000 a year.

Put another way, even if the Cybertruck goes away forever, Tesla is giving up very little to free up this space. Tesla's automotive sales revenue fell just 1% year over year in the third quarter. And its quarterly filing linked slightly lower deliveries mostly to fewer Model S and Model X sales.

Arguably, handing underused lines to new products is a sound move.

In Fremont, Tesla said in its third-quarter update that Optimus production had started on its high-volume lines, calling the bots coming off them its first production-quality robots. The plan, set out in January, is for that first line to one day make 1 million robots a year.

In Texas, Cybercab production began earlier this year on a line Tesla rates at over 125,000 vehicles a year, matching the Cybertruck line it'll take room from. Tesla has started adding these Cybercabs to its own Robotaxi fleet in Austin.

Neither product has its own revenue line in Tesla's results yet. Tesla took in around $104 billion in revenue over its past four reported quarters, and about 72% of it still came from its car business. The Model 3 and Model Y made up 98% of third-quarter deliveries. And total automotive revenue, which also includes regulatory credits, dropped 3% year over year in that quarter.

The stock, however, is priced as if both new products will succeed. With shares trading at around $358 as of this writing, Tesla's price-to-earnings ratio is above 160 based on the 2027 earnings forecast. By comparison, the forward price-to-earnings ratio of the S&P 500 (^GSPC +0.31%) is about 19.

A car business with falling revenue can't support a price-to-earnings ratio so high by itself. It only makes sense if Cybercab and Optimus grow into large, profitable businesses.

Sure, Tesla could pull it off. A robot line targeting 1 million units per year would be a massive business if demand materializes. But Optimus production has only just begun, and Tesla hasn't said what either new product earns.

Ultimately, the Cybertruck decision makes sense for the business. Still, it shows how much of the stock's value now depends on products for which Tesla doesn't yet report sales. Measured against Tesla's car business today, I think the stock is still far too expensive.

$150 in-stay credit when booking a stay of at least four nights.

Early check-in and late checkout, when available.

If you’re traveling by yourself or with a partner on a shorter trip, you might find more value staying at a hotel or resort that’s part of The Edit. You’ll get useful perks like complimentary breakfast for two and a $100 property credit.

Ultimately, the biggest benefit of adding vacation homes to The Edit is creating more booking options. If vacation homes fit your travel style, this is a great development to look forward to. If not, you’ll still be able to book hotels through The Edit like before.

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

Tomorrow, the Nerds will be watching the release of the October jobs report. If it shows that employment remained steady (or even improved), that will build a stronger case for the Federal Reserve to raise overnight borrowing rates again at their next meeting on Dec. 8-9.

While the Fed doesn’t directly set mortgage rates, it does set the federal funds rate, which is the fee that banks must pay to borrow from one another (which is how they fund mortgages). Lenders raise mortgage rates any time they think that the federal funds rate is about to go up.

Central bankers hiked the federal funds rate in September, so a relatively steady jobs report would suggest the labor market could withstand higher rates.

The Fed has a dual mandate to control inflation while supporting maximum employment, and raising the federal funds rate is their main tool for bringing inflation down. If they can work to lower inflation without hurting employment too badly, central bankers may feel more confident to act.

The September Personal Consumption Expenditures price index (PCE), the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, was released last Thursday. The data shows inflation was 3.6% year-over-year in September, up from 3.4% in August.

September’s federal funds rate hike came in the middle of the month, so October’s inflation data will really capture its effect on inflation. The October PCE report will come out on Nov. 25.

» Learn more: How the Fed affects mortgage rates

Refinancing might make sense if today’s rates are at least 0.5 to 0.75 of a percentage point lower than your current rate (and if you plan to stay in your home long enough to break even on closing costs).

With rates where they are right now, you may want to start considering a refi if your current rate is around 7.51% or higher — but there aren't too many people for whom that's true.

Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

If you're looking for a lower rate, use NerdWallet's refinance calculator to estimate savings and understand how long it would take to break even on the costs of refinancing.

» Time to refi? Compare refinance rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

There is no universal “right” time to start shopping — what matters is whether you can comfortably afford a mortgage now at today’s rates.

If the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget.

NerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a new home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings. Not only will this free up more cash flow for a future mortgage payment, it can also get you a better interest rate when you’re ready to buy.

» Is now a good time to buy? See NerdWallet’s analysis

If you already have a quote you’re happy with, you should consider locking your mortgage rate, especially if your lender offers a float-down option. A float-down lets you take advantage of a better rate if the market drops during your lock period.

Rate locks protect you from increases while your loan is processed, and with the market forever bouncing around, that peace of mind can be worth it.

🤓 Nerdy Reminder: Rates can change daily, and even hourly. If you’re happy with the deal you have, it’s okay to commit.

The rate you see advertised is a sample rate — usually for a borrower with perfect credit, making a big down payment, and paying for mortgage points. That won't match every buyer's circumstances.

In addition to market factors outside of your control, your customized quote depends on your:

Even two people with similar credit scores might get different rates, depending on their overall financial profiles.

» Get the best rate for you: How to get the best mortgage rate

Maybe — but even personalized rate quotes can change until you lock. That’s because lenders adjust pricing multiple times a day in response to market changes.

Democrats won big in the midterms, but mortgage rates have bigger forces to reckon with.

Mortgage rates fell again this week, extending a gradual slide that began well before Election Day.

The average rate on a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage fell 13 basis points to 7.05% APR in the week ending Nov. 5, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.) We calculate our weekly average using daily APRs recorded over the past five business days.

Homebuyers’ budgets are feeling the pinch from high mortgage rates, steep home prices and a shortage of listings. On the campaign trail, candidates from both parties promised to make homeownership more affordable. But solving that problem is like untangling 20 years’ worth of Christmas lights from your attic. Yank on one strand, and three more tighten.

“Jumpstarting the housing market relies on a calmer geopolitical environment and bond market in the short run and more housing supply plus a more dynamic labor market in the long run,” Jake Krimmel, senior economist for Realtor.com, said in an email.

A shift in political power won’t erase those challenges overnight. Here's what's driving mortgage rates right now — and where a Democratic Congress might have some pull.

How that affects mortgage rates: The relief of one less uncertainty is giving rates some breathing room.

Election results have cleared up one big unknown for investors. With Democrats controlling Congress and Republicans holding the White House, markets are bracing for the reality that any major spending bills could face roadblocks.

Political gridlock isn't always popular, but weirdly, investors sometimes welcome it. When a divided government limits new spending, the government may need to borrow less than expected — which could turn down the heat on mortgage rates.

But there’s a catch. That same gridlock could make it harder to pass laws to help bring down housing costs.

How that affects mortgage rates: Heavy borrowing from the government and tech companies adds upward pressure to the bond market, where mortgage rates take their cues.

When the government spends more than it collects in taxes, it borrows the difference by selling Treasury bonds. When there's lots of debt for sale, investors may demand higher returns, called yields. Mortgage rates tend to follow the yield on the 10-year Treasury note.

The new Congress still faces a mountain of government debt. What they choose to do about it can ripple through the economy to affect your monthly mortgage payment.

“Sound fiscal policy, rather than deficit-financed spending and standoffs over budgets and the debt limit, can help keep rates in check,” Andy Winkler, managing director for housing and infrastructure policy at the Bipartisan Policy Center, said in an email.

Meanwhile, Big Tech companies are borrowing a boatload of money to build AI data centers. To get the cash, they issue corporate bonds, giving investors another place to put their money. More bonds flooding the market can push Treasury yields higher, taking mortgage rates along for the ride.

But how long can the AI building boom last? Voters across party lines pushed back against data centers in the midterms. Even if lawmakers pump the brakes on new construction, a slowdown in tech spending doesn't guarantee cheaper mortgages.

How that affects mortgage rates: Wartime disruptions to global oil supplies can fuel inflation, pushing borrowing costs higher.

The unpopular war in Iran likely added to the voter frustration that helped fuel Democrats' midterm victories. Higher energy costs can hit household budgets in multiple ways: at the pump, through pricier goods that need to be shipped, and through higher interest rates on loans (including mortgages) as inflation heats up.

“A resolution would likely improve oil supply, helping to ease price pressures and potentially providing relief for mortgage rates,” Krimmel said.

A Democratic Congress could push for a different approach to ending the war, but it can't make Iran agree to a deal.

Meanwhile, stubborn inflation from the Iran war has raised the prospect of another Federal Reserve rate hike at its Dec. 8-9 meeting. Futures traders now put the odds of a quarter-point increase at more than 80%, according to CME FedWatch. The Fed doesn't set mortgage rates directly, but investors anticipate its decisions — so mortgage rates often move before the Fed does.

If buying a home makes sense for your budget now, there's little reason to wait just because Congress changed hands. Buyers can sometimes score lower prices in winter, when sellers are more willing to negotiate. But with today’s mortgage rates hovering above 7%, higher borrowing costs can eat into those savings, so it’s important to compare mortgage lenders to get the best rate.

For longer-term hope, look to the bipartisan 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which became law this summer. This legislation shows lawmakers can, in fact, work together to make meaningful progress on housing affordability.

“Even with divided government, lawmakers and the administration can build on that common ground to further boost housing production, preserve existing affordable homes, and help families struggling with high housing and utility costs,” Winkler said.

But new homes take time to build, and your house hunt doesn't have to follow Congress's calendar. Your homebuying budget and local market conditions matter more than the next political headline.

#3104. 2 Stocks Down 25% and 50% to Buy Now and Hold for the Next Decade.

Investors have punished PepsiCo and Hormel despite both being high-yield Dividend Kings.

Shares of PepsiCo (PEP -0.96%) are down 25% from their five-year high. That's bad, but it's even worse for Hormel (HRL -2.88%), which is down over 50% from its five-year high. Both companies are facing headwinds, but if history is any guide, they're worth buying and holding for the long term, given their historically high yields: 4.1% for PepsiCo and 5.1% for Hormel. Here's why.

PepsiCo and Hormel are unloved right now because they are both dealing with real headwinds. At the industry level, inflation is running high, putting pressure on profit margins while also causing consumers to tighten their budgets. Meanwhile, consumer buying habits are shifting toward healthier fare, which means food makers must invest to adjust their portfolios.

These are real problems and shouldn't be ignored. However, they are fairly normal problems in the consumer staples sector. Hormel and PepsiCo both have histories that go back more than 100 years. They have survived through periods like this before, and it is highly likely they will do so again.

That's underscored by the fact that both companies are Dividend Kings. That means they have increased their dividends annually for 50+ years. That isn't something that happens by accident; it requires a strong business model that gets executed well in both good times and bad. Now is just a bad time, but that's an opportunity if you like high-yield stocks.

PepsiCo will probably be the better choice for more conservative income investors. It operates globally, with businesses in the beverage, snack, and packaged-food spaces. It is the number one player in salty snacks and number two in beverages. The company has brand power, distribution might, marketing skills, and innovation chops that stand toe-to-toe with any consumer staples company.

In fact, despite current headwinds, the company's organic sales increased by 1.3% in the third quarter of 2026. Unfortunately, that was far below key competitor Coca-Cola (KO -0.06%), which saw organic sales grow 7% in the quarter. That has investors downbeat, but PepsiCo is still finding ways to grow. And eventually, the business is likely to pick up again. If you buy it today, you can collect that lofty yield while you wait.

Owning Hormel will take a bit more emotional resilience. While the yield is attractive, the company's organic sales fell 2% in the third quarter. That comes after a year or so of growth, suggesting that the company's turnaround efforts have hit a rough patch. But the Dividend King's food business is highly focused on protein, which puts it in a hot food trend. It also has a large business in the food service space, which has been performing quite well. In other words, there are both positives and negatives here.

That said, there's a unique twist that could make the stock a long-term buy. The Hormel Foundation owns roughly 47% of Hormel's stock. The foundation uses the dividends it collects to further its philanthropic efforts, so it wants to see a reliable and slowly growing dividend over time. That's basically what most dividend investors are likely to want as well, so you have an insider on your side. And a key purpose of the trust is to ensure that Hormel remains a stand-alone business, which means it has the leeway to make long-term investment decisions (regardless of Wall Street's typical near-term focus).

The S&P 500 index (^GSPC +0.31%) yields roughly 1%. The average consumer staples stock yields 2%. If you think in decades, even when Wall Street is thinking in days, buying high-yield Dividend Kings like PepsiCo and Hormel while they are out of favor can materially amp up your passive income stream. In fact, if you buy now, you may not want to sell when the businesses and stocks start to perk up again. Why give up such large yields from historically reliable dividend stocks when you have the opportunity to cash in on the dividends for decades to come?

#3102. The Yield vs. Weighting Dilemma: How to Choose Between SPSM and SCHA

State Street's fund holds fewer stocks but delivers higher income and lower volatility, while Schwab offers broader diversification across 1,750 holdings.

The State Street SPDR Portfolio S&P 600 Small Cap ETF (SPSM +0.06%) tracks a curated list of 608 small-cap stocks, while the Schwab U.S. Small-Cap ETF (SCHA +0.65%) offers much broader diversification across nearly 1,750 holdings.

Both exchange-traded funds provide low-cost access to U.S. small-cap stocks, yet they follow different indexing philosophies. While one focuses on the established S&P 600 index, the other tracks the Dow Jones U.S. Small-Cap Total Stock Market Index, leading to differences in sector weights and risk profiles.

Beta measures price volatility relative to the S&P 500; beta is calculated from monthly returns over the available fund history (up to five years). The 1-yr return represents total return over the trailing 12 months. Dividend yield is the trailing-12-month distribution yield.

Both funds are exceptionally affordable with identical 0.03% expense ratios. However, the State Street fund currently provides a higher income stream, outperforming the Schwab fund in trailing-12-month distribution yield by a modest margin.

Schwab U.S. Small-Cap ETF tracks a broad index of approximately 1,748 stocks, with its largest sectors including healthcare at 17%, financial services at 17%, and technology at 15%. Its largest positions include Halozyme Therapeutics (HALO -15.72%) at 0.36%, Glaukos (GKOS +2.01%) at 0.34%, and Wayfair (W -1.45%) at 0.32%. The fund was launched in 2009. Schwab U.S. Small-Cap ETF has paid $0.37 per share over the trailing 12 months, which, on its recent ~$33.05 share price, works out to a 1.1% yield.

State Street SPDR Portfolio S&P 600 Small Cap ETF holds 608 companies, leaning toward financial services at 18%, industrials at 17%, and consumer cyclical at 13%. Top holdings include Glaukos Corp at 0.81%, Viasat (VSAT +7.70%) at 0.61%, and Paycom Software (PAYC -5.08%) at 0.57%. The fund was launched in 2013. State Street SPDR Portfolio S&P 600 Small Cap ETF has paid $0.82 per share over the trailing 12 months, which, at its recent ~$54.98 share price, works out to a 1.5% yield.

For more guidance on ETF investing, check out the full guide at this link.

When comparing the State Street SPDR Portfolio S&P 600 Small Cap ETF (SPSM) and the Schwab U.S. Small-Cap ETF (SCHA), investors should consider several key factors. Let's see what they tell us about each fund.

First, we should examine each fund's strategy. SPSM is focused on profitable small-cap companies. It holds about 600 stocks. SCHA, on the other hand, casts a wider net, holding about 1,700 small-cap stocks.

Two other important factors are historical performance and income potential. Since 2021, SPSM has generated a total return of 24%, equating to a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 4.4%. SCHA, by contrast, has delivered a total return of 26%, with a 4.8% CAGR. Neither fund has matched the S&P 500's performance over this stretch. As for income, SPSM has the higher yield, at 1.5%; SCHA's 1.1% still offers some cash flow to income-focused investors.

One final factor to weigh is cost. Here, both funds excel. They each offer a matching annual expense ratio of 0.03%, making both funds excellent choices for cost-conscious investors.In summary, SPSM and SCHA are both small-cap index ETFs, yet they do exhibit some key differences. SPSM holds fewer stocks, but is actually less top-heavy. SCHA holds three times as many stocks as SPSM, but its weighting system means that its top 10 stocks contribute around 10% of its exposure. With historical performance and cost essentially a push, the head-to-head matchup largely comes down to income potential and investor preference. Many investors will favor SPSM for its higher dividend yield, yet SCHA is a fine choice for those who prefer its methodology.

The right card for you may depend on where you travel, how often, and your level of elite status with Bonvoy.

Two of the popular credit cards in the Marriott Bonvoy portfolio deliver various benefits to their users. The right one for you may depend on your typical travel patterns and history, such as if you already have a high level of elite status with Marriott or you travel only to certain regions.

The Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card and the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card both come with valuable perks, but there are quite a few considerations that are worth a thorough review. Many travelers prefer not to have two cards from the same loyalty program, and these two cards are actually quite different from each other (including being issued by different banks).

Let’s take a look at these two Marriott co-branded cards to see if one may serve your needs over the other.

Here's how the cards stack up on the basics.

Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card

While the “winning” card for some may not apply to everyone, we wanted to analyze the card that provides exceptional benefits for travelers looking for a Marriott card in exchange for the cost of the annual fee. Those new to Marriott will find this to be a solid entry-level card, but it also works for Marriott Bonvoy fans looking for some extra perks without a huge outlay of money for an annual fee. These are the benefits that handed this card the win.

The annual fee on the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card is notably less at $95 compared with $250 on the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card. While the earning rates when using the card to pay for Marriott stays are nearly the same, and both have bonus categories where you can earn multiples of points based on everyday spending, the lower-annual-fee card offers a lot of points earning for its low annual fee.

On top of the lower annual fee, it comes with an automatic annual free night award, Silver Elite status and a fast path to achieve Gold if you use the card often. Add to that an annual $100 in airline credits and DoorDash DashPass membership, and you have more than covered the annual fee without considering the other perks.

The Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card card’s $250 annual fee is higher, and its annual free night award requires spending $15,000 in eligible purchases. But the card comes with automatic Gold Elite status and more bonus points earned.

There are other cards (like American Express Platinum Card®) that also include free Gold Elite status with Marriott that can provide decent value for their annual fee (enrollment required). From a pure cash maximization perspective, the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card wins because it provides more bang for your buck.

The Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card is the only one of the two cards to include an annual free night award, and it has a lower annual fee. It can be used at properties up to 35,000 points a night. This can render great value and is more than worth the $95 annual fee. Hands down, it is the winner in this category.

If you spend more than $15,000 on the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card in a calendar year, you can unlock a free night certificate valid at up to 50,000 points. This is even more valuable than the included certificate that comes with the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card, but it also requires you to spend more on this card to get it.

It is important to consider the opportunity cost of not putting certain types of spend on other cards where you could be earning greater multiples of points for the same type of spending. Would losing those points be worth the value of a one-night-free certificate? Since Marriott relies on dynamic pricing, which means that points rates for a redemption night can fluctuate regularly, in many cases the value may not reach the level of the missed points opportunity.

While both cards offer decent travel protection benefits, only the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card comes with a flight credit. You can earn up to $100 in statement credits when making purchases directly with airlines by spending $250 on the card before the end of 2026 for a $50 statement credit and another $50 credit by spending $50 before June 30, 2027. That gives another point to the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card Boundless card.

» Learn more: Should I be loyal to a single airline?

If you don’t already have a Marriott co-branded credit card and you want to diversify what’s in your wallet, this could be a great option for big spenders. And if you are looking for one of the fastest paths to high Marriott elite status, this card can help you get there.

Both the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card and Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card cards offer bonus points on spending, but the more expensive annual fee Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card card offers more points on more spending opportunities, including the below:

18.5X points on Marriott Bonvoy property spending (1.5X more than the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card card).

4X points at global restaurants, including U.S. takeout and delivery plus U.S. Supermarkets on up to $15,000 in combined purchases, then 2X points (that’s 1X more than what Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card offers and available on $9,000 more in spending).

1,000 bonus points when staying at a Marriott Bonvoy property.

Depending on how much you spend in these categories, you have the ability to earn more points with this card than the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card, including when you are not traveling. And then when you are, you earn 1,000 Marriott bonus points for each paid, eligible stay booked directly with Marriott. This gives it an edge, even though the annual fee is higher.

When you get the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card, you’ll receive 15 elite night credits deposited into your Marriott account. This is on top of the instant Gold Elite status you earn with the card, which normally requires staying 25 nights. To reach the next tier, Platinum, you only need an additional 10 nights to reach its 50-night minimum.

This means not only do you start out at a higher elite tier with Marriott just for having this card, but also you can progress more quickly to Platinum. For frequent travelers, the best value of this card is the opportunity to reach the next status tier faster. And if you wanted to keep going, you would only need 35 more nights to get to Titanium, which is rich with on-property perks like lounge access, welcome gifts and room upgrades.

Earning these nights within a calendar year is not difficult for Marriott loyalists, especially if you hit the jackpot during a promotion that offers double elite nights.

The status perks don’t stop there. Once you hit Marriott’s Titanium status, you can then link your account with United Airlines to earn United’s Premier Silver elite status for more benefits when you fly United, including greater baggage allowance and free extra-legroom economy seats at check-in.

Both of these cards provide Marriott Bonvoy points earning and elite status, and they both offer a great way to expedite points earning or receive travel and purchase protections when using the card. But the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card packs a greater punch in its benefits for a lower annual fee. It becomes a great additional card to others you may have (like the American Express Platinum Card®, which has its own impressive travel perk lineup).

If you are a Marriott frequent guest, the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card offers higher-tier Gold status and a faster path to even better tiers for perks. But, it costs more each year and does not offer a free annual night.

Deciding which perks are more important for you, as well as looking at what benefits come from other cards in your wallet, will help you make an informed decision on which of the two best suits your needs.

#3100. Coupang vs. GameStop: Which Consumer Stock Is a Better Buy Going Into 2027?

Coupang's P/S ratio sits far below GameStop's, while GameStop's cash-heavy balance sheet and thin-margin logistics bet tell very different stories.

Investors looking for retail sector exposure face a choice between rapid digital expansion and a legacy chain's turnaround. Choosing between Coupang (CPNG -0.79%) and GameStop (GME +3.93%) requires weighing high-growth logistics against a cash-heavy balance sheet.

Coupang dominates the South Korean e-commerce market with its proprietary logistics network, offering ultra-fast delivery. GameStop, once a mall-based video game retailer, is pivoting toward collectibles and digital assets while managing a massive cash pile. Both are significant players among retail stocks seeking to capture evolving consumer habits in the digital age.

Coupang is a technology-driven company that provides retail, restaurant delivery, video streaming, and fintech services. It operates a two-sided marketplace that connects over 25 million active customers with a vast array of suppliers and merchants. The company relies on its WOW membership program, and partners with various international manufacturers, such as Sartori Cheese, to export perishable goods to South Korea via its Rocket Fresh platform.

In its 2025 fiscal year (FY), revenue reached $34.5 billion, which represents a growth of 14.1% compared to the prior year. The company reported a net income of $208.0 million for the period, resulting in a net margin of 0.6%. This trend shows continued revenue expansion and consistent profitability compared to the $154.0 million in net income reported in the previous fiscal year.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was 1.0x, meaning total debt is roughly equal to shareholder equity. The current ratio is 1.0x, indicating the company has just enough short-term assets to cover its immediate liabilities. Free cash flow for the year was $522.0 million. Note that stock-based compensation (SBC) represented 26.8% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

GameStop is a specialty retailer that offers video games, collectibles, and entertainment products through a global network of over 2,000 stores. The company serves its customer base through physical locations and e-commerce platforms, supported by loyalty programs like GameStop Pro. It also operates trade-in programs for used hardware and graded trading cards to maintain its relevance in the gaming community.

In FY 2025, ended on Jan. 31 of this year, revenue was $3.6 billion, representing a decline of 5.1% compared to the previous year. Despite the lower sales, the company achieved a net income of $418.4 million for the period. This resulted in a net margin of 11.5%, which is a significant improvement over the net margin reported in the prior fiscal year.

As of its January 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was 0.8x, meaning total debt is approximately 80% of shareholder equity. The current ratio is 15.3x, which is a measure of liquidity showing the company has over 15 times more current assets than current liabilities. Free cash flow for the fiscal year was $597.3 million, providing the company with substantial capital to fund its strategic initiatives.

GameStop deals with high stock price volatility that is often driven by speculative trading and short squeezes rather than business fundamentals. The company relies heavily on the strategic leadership of Ryan Cohen and must navigate a cyclical gaming industry that is shifting toward digital downloads from competitors like Microsoft (MSFT -0.99%). Its investment policy includes exposure to Bitcoin (BTC -0.02%), which introduces additional market volatility. Furthermore, the company faces challenges with its retail footprint and the execution of its attempted eBay (EBAY -1.13%) acquisition, which has shifted from a takeover bid to a potential partnership after eBay's Board of Directors rejected GameStop's buyout offer.

Coupang features a much lower P/S ratio than GameStop, though its Forward P/E is significantly higher due to thinner net margins.

Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.

Between retail giants Coupang and GameStop, I would buy the former. That said, Coupang's sales growth was hampered after a cyberattack compromised customer data in its core South Korea market last year. While it ended 2025 with 14% year-over-year revenue growth, that slowed to 8% in the first quarter of 2026, then dropped to 4% in Q2.

Coupang's Q3 results suggest it may have turned a corner on regaining customer trust. Its Q3 sales rose 7% year over year to $10 billion. If this performance extends into subsequent quarters, it suggests the black eye from the data breach may be behind it, making Coupang a stock to own.

The problem with GameStop is that it has yet to prove it possesses a sustainable business model. Its year-over-year sales decline in FY 2025 continues in 2026. In the company's fiscal Q2, ended Aug. 1, it reported sales of $790.2 million, a steep decline from the prior year's $972.2 million. Revenue fell due to store closures and the divestiture of its operations in France. Until GameStop can find a way to return to sustainable sales growth, Coupang is the superior stock.

#3099. As AI becomes more fractured, one name stands out: AMD

As Anthropic rushes to takes its shares public, the AI trade is showing cracks, and they are not confined to fringe players.

We recently wrote about CoreWeave, which fell 15.5% on Oct. 14 as yields on its 2032 notes touched 15%, and its default-swap spreads nearly doubled in October. IREN is down more than 20% this year. Last Thursday, the contagion reached chipmakers, which makes sense since much of CRWV and IREN's spending is going there. AMD dropped 8.1% as Meta's financing plans and a supply warning from Lam Research exacerbated data-center fears about the pace of AI spending.

Because when you screen for factors that demonstrably generate outperformance over time, the list narrows quickly. My screen: price above the 200-day moving average; revenue growing at least as fast as the S&P 500 (5%+ per annum); EPS growing at least as fast (7%+); rating upgrades; a PEG below 3; and ROE and ROIC of at least 12%. Of the names reporting in the next two weeks, AMD is effectively the only one that makes the list. Yes, you can (and arguably should, as our staples article described) position your portfolio with slightly less tech exposure than the broad indices provide, but we can't ignore the market's biggest and most transformative sector entirely.

Especially because the growth in this case doesn't just meet my criteria; it blows past them. Consensus for Q3 calls for EPS of $1.94 on revenue of $13.06 billion, versus $1.20 and $9.25 billion a year ago. That's YoY growth of nearly 62% and 41%, respectively. The recent drawdown came from a sector selloff, not anything AMD reported, but it shows that if some names in the space get hit, even the larger players are likely to feel it. On Oct. 6, Lisa Su said AMD would substantially increase supply in 2027 because AI orders keep outrunning capacity.

So how do you balance factors we know work for a fast-growing company against a backdrop of cracks in the AI trade? Options.

Owning the stock outright means absorbing a roughly 9% to 11% implied earnings-related move (day of). Earnings are about a week out, and over the past four quarters the smallest move over a similar window was more than 9%, and the largest move, after the company reported its Q1 26 results, was 38%! Of course, that kind of volatility means options aren't cheap, and that rich premium is also a reason not to simply buy calls.

A call spread risk reversal does both jobs: it reduces risk if the cracks widen, and the short options offset the elevated volatility we would otherwise pay for. The bottom chart shows that, by sacrificing about $1,700 of upside for $5,000 in outperformance during a severe downside move, and given how jittery this trade has been lately, this is a way to stay in it with considerably less risk. $5,000 less, specifically. Of course, selling that out will tie up some cash, but less so than simply buying the stock. And selling both the out and the call reduces long call purchase by 66%

Each year, the IRS adjusts tax brackets to keep pace with inflation. The 2027 tax brackets were announced on Nov. 5, 2026.

The IRS has released updated tax brackets for 2027, which apply to the taxes we file in 2028. You may notice that the seven tax rates generally stay the same year-to-year — so why do tax brackets get adjusted?

Well, due to inflation, our money might not stretch as far as it did the previous year. To combat that, the IRS adjusts tax brackets so taxpayers can keep a little bit more of their money in a lower tax bracket compared with the previous year.

For example, a single filer could make up to $50,400 in 2026 and pay a top tax rate of 12%. But in 2027, they could make up to $52,025 and still only pay a top tax rate of 12% thanks to these inflation adjustments.

Not sure how to read the tax bracket tables below?

Find your total taxable income in the "tax bracket" column. The corresponding tax rate is the highest rate you'll pay — it doesn’t apply to all your income; it applies only to the portion that falls within that bracket. The income in the lower brackets is taxed at those lower rates.

For example, let's say you’re a single filer and you expect to earn $150,000 this year. The top rate you’d pay on a portion of your income is 24%. The rest would be taxed at 10%, 12% and 22%.

#3097. Here's What the Average Social Security Benefit Actually Covers

The average Social Security check covers only a fraction of what seniors actually spend each year.

Most retirees lean on Social Security for much of their income, yet the average check was built to replace only part of a paycheck. As of September 2026, the average retired-worker benefit is $2,088.79 per month, according to the Social Security Administration (SSA) Monthly Statistical Snapshot. That adds up to $25,065.48 per year.

A household headed by someone 65 or older spends $61,432 per year, based on the BLS Consumer Expenditure Survey from 2024, the most recent data available. While housing and healthcare are major concerns, transportation and food costs also represent significant portions of a typical senior's budget.

The average annual benefit of $25,065.48 covers only 41% of that annual senior-household spending. This is by design, as the government built the program to replace roughly 40% of pre-retirement income. It's not intended to fund a complete lifestyle on its own.

The SSA calculates your benefit based on your highest 35 years of earnings, where earlier wages are adjusted for inflation, through the primary insurance amount (PIA) formula. This leaves an annual shortfall of $36,366.52 that you'll need to cover through other sources.

For retirees without a pension or deep savings, part-time work may be the only realistic way to fill that hole. Inflation adjustments provide some relief, but they're meant to maintain current buying power rather than increase it.

A 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) will take effect in 2027, adding about $75 a month to that average check. This adjustment is designed to help your benefits keep pace with rising prices. The average check is a foundation, not a full budget, and the question is how to cover the rest.

It's possible to beat the average Social Security check by delaying your Social Security application. Every month you wait to apply increases your monthly benefits until you qualify for your largest checks at 70.

If you expect to have an average or above-average life expectancy and you can afford to cover your living costs another way in the meantime, delaying your Social Security application is a viable way to grow your checks. It could also lead to a much larger lifetime benefit.

Things like remaining in the workforce for longer or increasing your income today could also lead to larger Social Security checks in the future because the SSA bases your benefit on your average monthly income over your 35 highest-earning years. If you're earning more now than in years past, working a bit longer could boost your future benefits.

But even in the best-case scenario, your checks likely won't be enough to cover all your living expenses in retirement. Make sure you have a plan for how you'll cover what Social Security doesn't before you sign up.

For more on how Social Security affects your retirement, see this guide.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

Here's a rundown of changes to some well-known tax provisions for the 2027 tax year.

Each year, the IRS updates common tax provisions, such as income tax brackets and the standard deduction, to ensure the tax code is keeping pace with the rising cost of living.

These tweaks — formally known as inflation adjustments — help prevent “bracket creep,” where taxpayers who received a cost-of-living raise can pay more in taxes even though their purchasing power remains unchanged.

Inflation adjustments for the 2027 tax year were set at 3.2% — larger than the previous two years as inflation heated up. This could mean lower tax bills for some people when they file in 2028.

In the U.S., there are seven marginal rates — 10%, 12%, 22%, 24%, 32%, 35% and 37% — which will remain unchanged for 2027.

Contrary to a popular myth, it’s uncommon for people to pay a single flat federal tax rate on their taxable income. Instead, portions of a person’s income can be taxed at different rates depending on which tax brackets they fall into. For example, some of a person’s income could be taxed at 10%, another chunk at 12%, and so on.

For 2027, the IRS is adjusting those tax brackets — the windows of income that dictate where a tax rate ends and begins — for each filing status. The adjustments mean that some people may be able to keep some of their income in lower tax brackets, and those who received a cost-of-living raise may avoid getting a portion of their income pushed into a higher bracket.

Married filers, for example, can make up to $104,050 to remain with a top tax rate of 12%, compared with $100,800 in 2026. This increase could allow some couples to shelter an additional $3,250 from a higher tax rate in 2027.

2026 vs. 2027 tax brackets: Single filers

2026 vs. 2027 tax brackets: Heads of household

2026 vs. 2027 tax brackets: Married filing separately

» MORE: See the full 2027 tax brackets for each filing status

The IRS lets most filers lower their taxable income by taking the standard deduction or itemizing their returns. The standard deduction, a flat amount based on filing status and age, is popular, as it requires less work to claim and is often more beneficial for those who might not have deductible expenses.

For 2027, the standard deduction will be $16,600 for single filers and those married filing separately, a $500 increase from 2026. Joint filers will be eligible to take $33,200 and heads of household can take $24,925, a $1,000 and $775 increase over 2026, respectively.

» Need help deciding whether to itemize or take the standard deduction? Learn about the differences

Also included in the IRS' 32-page inflation release are various updates to several tax provisions beyond the federal tax brackets. Plus, a brand-new tax credit will go into effect in 2027.

Starting in 2027, taxpayers who contribute to a health flexible spending account (FSA) can contribute up to $3,500 and, if their plan permits, carry over up to $700 into the next tax year.

For those with health savings accounts, the 2027 limit for contributions will rise to $4,500 for self-only coverage and $9,000 for family coverage.

The annual exclusion for gifts, which limits how much taxpayers can give an individual without filing a gift tax return on certain gifts, will be $20,000 per person in 2027, an increase of $1,000 compared with 2026.

The lifetime estate tax exclusion establishes a threshold for the taxation of estates upon a person's death. In 2027, estates valued at or below $15.48 million will not be subject to estate tax, up from $15 million in 2026.

The Education Freedom Tax Credit will launch on Jan. 1. According to the IRS, it aims to support private contributions for K-12 scholarships. Taxpayers who donate to a "scholarship granting organization" in one of the 30 participating states can receive a nonrefundable tax credit of up to $1,700 ($3,400 for couples filing jointly).

#3093. Novo Nordisk Just Delivered Great News for Investors. Is a Comeback Finally Underway?

Novo got a much-needed boost from its latest earnings report.

Are things finally starting to look up for Novo (NVO +0.03%)? The Denmark-based pharmaceutical leader has had a rough past couple of years, but its third-quarter financial results were strong enough to send the stock up 6% post-earnings. That's great news for shareholders, but can Novo maintain this momentum?

At first glance, Novo's third-quarter results didn’t seem particularly impressive, as some of the company’s longtime growth drivers underperformed. For instance, sales of Ozempic, the company's famous diabetes medicine, were 29.7 billion Danish kroner (about $4.5 billion), down 3% compared to the year-ago period. The company's weight-loss medicine, Wegovy, recorded sales of 20.4 billion DKK (about $3.1 billion), roughly flat compared with the prior-year quarter.

However, several other medicines helped pick up the slack, and arguably none was more important than Novo's oral Wegovy. The company launched this weight loss pill -- the first of its kind to earn approval -- in January. The Wegovy pill has helped attract many patients who were hesitant to start treatment with injectables. Novo reported that, as of June, oral Wegovy had surpassed three million prescriptions, and more than 80% were for patients who had never taken GLP-1s before. In the third quarter, oral Wegovy generated 5.4 billion DKK (about $810 million) in revenue.

Novo's total net sales were 79.2 billion DKK (about $11.9 billion), up 6% year over year. The company's net income dropped by 16% year over year to 16.7 billion DKK (about $2.5 billion), largely due to non-cash impairment charges. Still, Novo’s results beat analyst estimates, and the pharmaceutical company also raised its guidance for the fiscal year 2026.

It now expects revenue to be flat (at the midpoint) year over year, while the previous guidance implied a 3% year-over-year drop at the midpoint. It's no wonder Novo's shares jumped following this beat-and-raise quarter. But what's next for the drugmaker?

There are several catalysts ahead that could help Novo improve its financial performance. Let's consider three of them. First, the company could make meaningful progress with oral Wegovy. The medicine has now been approved in several other countries, including Germany and the U.K.

These markets might not be as lucrative as the U.S., but they should move the needle for the company. Novo will also likely attract brand-new GLP-1 patients in these regions. The company is also looking to earn label expansions for oral Wegovy. Novo has submitted an application to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration for oral Wegovy as a potential treatment for metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis.

The original injectable version of Wegovy is approved for this indication, but the pill offers a more convenient option. It could be successful in this niche and continue driving Novo's sales higher. Second, Novo will launch new products to strengthen its position in the diabetes and weight-loss markets.

It is inching closer to approval for CagriSema, a medicine that beat Wegovy in a head-to-head Phase 3 clinical trial for weight loss. CagriSema also posted strong clinical trial results in diabetes. This medicine could help Novo steal some market share from its biggest competitor, Eli Lilly (LLY -0.79%).

Third, Novo has several pipeline candidates that could improve its approved lineup over time. The company's Phase 3 pipeline features zenagamtide, a promising diabetes and weight-loss medicine that is being developed in subcutaneous and oral formulations.

The weight loss market is growing rapidly, and this product, along with others, may help Novo ride that tailwind for a long time, even as competition intensifies. Novo may still experience some clinical setbacks, but after the beating it took over the past two years, the company is slowly staging a comeback. In my view, the stock is attractive following its third-quarter results.

#3089. Magnite vs. Reddit: Which Media Stock Is a Better Buy Going Into 2027?

Reddit's revenue surged far faster than Magnite's last year, yet only one of these ad stocks trades at a meaningfully lower forward earnings multiple.

As digital advertising shifts away from traditional formats, investors must decide which platforms can best navigate the changing landscape. Choosing between Magnite (MGNI -0.47%) and Reddit (RDDT +1.38%) depends on your preferred growth strategy.

Magnite serves as a vital middleman for publishers looking to sell digital ad space, while Reddit offers a massive community-driven platform for direct engagement. Both companies represent different segments of the modern advertising ecosystem.

Magnite operates as the world's largest independent sell-side advertising company. It provides the technology that helps publishers monetize their content across connected TV, online video, and display formats. The company serves major partners like LG Electronics-owned LG Ad Solutions, and recently partnered with OpenAI to boost ad placements within ChatGPT.

In its latest annual report, filed for its 2025 fiscal year (FY), revenue reached nearly $714.0 million. This represents revenue growth of 6.9% compared to the previous year. Magnite reported net income of $144.6 million for the period, which resulted in a net margin of 20.3%.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was 0.7x. This metric compares total debt to shareholder equity to show how much a company relies on borrowing. The current ratio, which measures the ability to cover short-term debts with short-term assets, stands at 1.0x. Free cash flow was $165.6 million. Note that stock-based compensation (SBC) represented 32.5% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

Reddit is a prominent name for those investing in social media stocks. It generates most of its revenue from third-party advertising, but it has also expanded into content licensing for training generative artificial intelligence models. The platform reported 130.3 million daily active unique (DAUq) users as of the third quarter of 2026, showing its massive reach.

In its latest annual report, filed for FY 2025, revenue reached $2.2 billion. This reflects significant revenue growth of 69.4% over the prior year. Reddit reported net income of $529.7 million, delivering a net margin of 24.1% as it transitioned into profitability.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the company carried a debt-to-equity ratio of zero. Its current ratio was 11.6x, indicating a strong ability to meet short-term obligations. Free cash flow reached $684.2 million for the year. Note that stock-based compensation represented 49.7% of operating cash flow.

Magnite faces significant revenue concentration, with two buyers indirectly contributing about 44% of its total revenue. Its success depends heavily on the growth of the connected TV market and continued access to that inventory. The company also deals with intense competition from Alphabet (GOOGL +0.78%), Amazon (AMZN -0.35%), and Comcast (CMCSA -2.24%). Furthermore, ongoing litigation with Alphabet's Google regarding anticompetitive practices remains a potential financial risk.

Reddit relies on its ability to maintain user engagement and contributions, which are the primary drivers of its advertising value. The company faces concentration risks, as its top ten advertisers account for roughly 21% of total revenue. Its community-led moderation model can lead to disruptions that may alienate advertisers or users. Additionally, Reddit depends on infrastructure provided by third-party cloud services from Amazon and Alphabet to remain operational.

Reddit stock trades at a lower multiple of future earnings estimates, while Magnite appears more attractively priced based on its sales over the past twelve months.

Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.

Between Magnite and Reddit, I would prioritize investing in Reddit. Both rely on digital advertising to fund their businesses, but Reddit's consumer-facing community platform gives it the edge.

The company's 130.3 million DAUq users in Q3 represented strong 12% year-over-year growth, indicating Reddit continues to attract an engaged user base. This makes the social media giant a compelling place for advertisers to spend their budgets. Consequently, the company grew Q3 revenue by a whopping 53% year over year to $895 million.

Reddit stock is also much cheaper based on its forward earnings multiple, and while its sales multiple is a bit higher than Magnite's, the company's much faster revenue growth signals that it's business is still rapidly expanding. Magnite's Q3 sales of $204.2 million represented an excellent 14% year-over-year increase, but is still much lower than Reddit's 53%.

The one important downside to note is that Reddit's reliance on search engines to deliver traffic to its site is at risk with the artificial intelligence boom. Users are increasingly looking to AI when performing searches, bringing a drop to traditional search visits. Reddit is responding by testing a requirement for users to log in when visiting the site, which prevents AI from taking its content.

#3086. Ripple strikes deal with Robinhood to expand its RLUSD digital dollar

Ripple has struck a deal with Robinhood to expand the reach of its digital dollar, RLUSD, strengthening trading and financing links between their institutional businesses and improving Robinhood's internal money management.

The partnership involves using RLUSD to settle institutional trades, automate Robinhood's treasury operations and expand access to digital asset trading and financing through Ripple Prime and Bitstamp, the global crypto exchange acquired by Robinhood last year.

It also helps meet Robinhood's ambition of becoming a global financial superapp, centralizing its customers' financial lives while expanding the underlying infrastructure that can serve both retail and institutional clients.

"Utility is what moves stablecoins forward. Working with Ripple, Bitstamp and Robinhood will have access to RLUSD for institutional settlement, Ripple Treasury for our operations and Ripple Prime for financing," Robinhood Crypto General Manager Johann Kerbrat said in a statement shared with CNBC. "That is what a connected, global financial system looks like."

Stablecoins have long been a workhorse of the crypto world, giving traders a way to move money among exchanges, buy and sell crypto assets, and park funds between trades without having to convert back into traditional currency. But as the crypto industry evolves beyond trading and markets move toward 24/7 liquidity, stablecoins are becoming essential financial infrastructure because of their ability to enable near-instant settlement and move dollar-denominated value at any time, regardless of traditional banking hours.

As firms look to do more with stablecoins beyond simply listing them on exchanges, stablecoin issuers are betting they'll favor a one-stop-shop approach that bundles the technology and services needed to move money, settle trades and manage cash.

"Stablecoins have evolved from a crypto trading tool into a critical piece of financial infrastructure," Ripple President Monica Long told CNBC. "The clearest evidence of this is where they're now being embedded — from corporate payments to capital markets. Our partnership with Robinhood reflects that evolution."

"This is about much more than trading," she added. "It's about fundamentally changing how money moves and is managed — giving institutions the ability to operate 24/7/365, unlocking liquidity and putting capital to work more efficiently."

Circle Internet Group, a Ripple competitor, is positioning itself for a similar future, where winning platforms, in addition to issuing stablecoins, also provide the infrastructure to put them to work. Earlier this year, for example, it launched the Circle Payments Network, connecting financial institutions and payment providers using its flagship USDC stablecoin and other digital assets for cross-border payments.

The network is Circle's answer to the 8-year-old Ripple Payments business, a service that helps businesses move money across borders, using any of several assets moving through that system, including USDC, Ripple-created XRP and, as of its debut in December 2024, RLUSD.

RLUSD's market cap has grown to more than $2.5 billion. Tether's USDT and Circle's USDC still dominate the total stablecoin market, which now exceeds $300 billion.

RLUSD will also be listed on Robinhood's trading platform, and is currently available to traders on Bitstamp as well as Robinhood Chain, the company's home-grown blockchain for tokenized stocks and other assets.

Robinhood, which reports third-quarter results for the three months ended in September after the market closes, rose about 2.5% in early trading Tuesday, snapping a three-day decline.

Correction: A previous headline misspelled RLUSD.
