Basic economy tickets come with plenty of restrictions, but holding the right credit card is my top trick for avoiding some of them.

As airfares remain high, that basic economy fare might look more tempting than ever. Saving $100 on a round-trip domestic flight could mean more money for hotels, dining or other experiences at your destination.

I’ve flown my fair share of basic economy flights, which come with restrictions like being unable to select a seat, earning no award miles and boarding last. You also can’t make changes or cancel your itinerary without paying a hefty fee, and — specific to United Airlines — you can’t bring a full-size carry-on on board.

But as a United frequent flyer, I have a secret to share with you: Holding the United℠ Explorer Card (annual fee: $0 intro for the first year, then $150) lets you avoid several of those basic economy restrictions.

Right now, new United℠ Explorer Card applicants can receive this welcome offer: Earn 70,000 bonus miles after you spend $3,000 on purchases in the first 3 months your account is open. Plus, earn 10,000 bonus miles when you add an authorized user in the first 3 months your account is open.

Most major airlines no longer let you earn points or miles on basic economy fares. United is an exception, though — assuming you hold the right credit card.

Eligible cardholders, including those who have the United℠ Explorer Card, earn at least 3 miles per $1 spent on United basic economy tickets, excluding taxes and select fees. That’s half of what a standard economy ticket earns for cardholders (6 miles per $1), but it’s better than zero. If you have elite status, you’ll earn more.

Those miles are in addition to the 3 miles per $1 you earn on all United purchases when using your United℠ Explorer Card.

With the card, your miles can become more valuable. That’s because cardholders get at least 10% off award tickets that are operated by United or United Express. If you have United status, that discount gets bumped up to at least 15% off.

With the credit card, you have access to priority boarding in Group 2. That means you’ll be able to board earlier compared to the rest of the basic economy passengers in Group 6, making it more likely you’ll find space for your carry-on bag.

Now, you might be thinking: Wait a minute… Basic economy doesn’t allow you to bring a carry-on bag. Let me explain how that works.

United enforces its full-size carry-on restriction based on your boarding group. Group 6 passengers can't bring a full-size carry-on.

Because the credit card gets you Group 2 boarding, you essentially skip that restriction.

Premier members — who board in Group 2 or earlier — are also exempt from the full-size carry-on restriction when flying basic economy.

If you don’t want to deal with the hassle of a carry-on bag, you can opt to check it instead.

As long as you pay for your ticket using your United℠ Explorer Card, you’ll be able to check your first bag — and your companion’s first bag — for free when traveling on United. (If you’re booking an award ticket, make sure to use your card to pay for the taxes and fees.)

Keep in mind that if the first flight on your itinerary is operated by another airline, that airline’s baggage rules would apply and you would have to pay for your bag.

Of course, holding the right United credit card only gets you so far.

With basic economy, you’ll still need to pay a fee to change or cancel your ticket, and you won’t be able to select a seat for free.

Ultimately, whether basic economy is a good deal depends on a few factors.

If your plans might change, pay up for standard economy. Otherwise, the penalty to change or cancel will end up costing you more than you saved.

Another thing to consider is whether you’re willing to sit in a middle seat. You might be fine with it for a few hours, but what about a long-haul flight to Asia? Everyone’s threshold is different, so you’ll need to decide whether the middle-seat gamble is worth it.

If your plans are firm and you don’t mind a potential middle seat, booking a basic economy ticket can be a solid way to save money. Just book with a United card like, the United℠ Explorer Card, to avoid the biggest downsides.

#3079. Energy Transfer Just Raised Its Distribution for the 20th Straight Quarter. Here's How Much $10,000 Invested Pays Annually.

Don't let a past dividend cut scare you away from this 7%-yielding pipeline stock.

Energy Transfer (ET -1.41%), one of the largest pipeline-focused master limited partnerships (MLPs), recently announced its 20th consecutive increase in its quarterly cash distribution. Raising its quarterly distribution by more than 3%, the company now pays $0.3425 per unit quarterly, or $1.37 per unit annually.

That said, given how Energy Transfer has implemented a dividend cut in the recent past, management's touting of its "20th consecutive quarterly increase" is a bit misleading. Yet, while Energy Transfer may lack the dividend growth track record of other pipeline stocks, that doesn't mean you need to stick this name in your "stay away" pile.

Based on Energy Transfer's current stock price of around $19 per share, a $10,000 investment would buy you around 526 units. Multiply that by the annualized distributions, and the total amount of distributions from this investment is around $720 per year.

This equates to around a 7.1% forward distribution yield, well above the S&P 500 current forward dividend yield of around 1.1%. This also represents a higher forward yield than peers, such as 6.1%-yielding Enterprise Products Partners and 5.7%-yielding Enbridge.

Energy Transfer may have cut distributions in the past, but I wouldn't anticipate this happening again anytime soon. For one, Energy Transfer's distribution cut was due primarily to the COVID-19 outbreak, a black swan event. Moreover, consider Energy Transfer's latest quarterly results. For the quarter ending Sept. 30, the MLP reported distributable cash flow of $2.5 billion versus $1.18 billion in distributions.

Energy Transfer is also pursuing acquisitions it believes are accretive to its distributable cash flow, such as its recently announced $2.6 billion deal for Vaquero Midstream, and continues to invest billions organically to expand its pipeline network. Although future performance hinges heavily on the macro backdrop for energy, until signs of an unfavorable shift emerge, consider Energy Transfer another top choice among pipeline stocks for income-focused investors.

#3077. We Write About Saving Money; Here’s How We Trick Our Brains Into Doing It

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

Even personal finance writers and editors need psychological hacks to save money. Here are the tips we use, and why they work.

While staring at the Container Store cart on my phone at 11 p.m., I did something for the first time that I’d read about a hundred times. Instead of spending $200 on more organizational boxes that I categorically did not need, I transferred that amount to my savings account.

Normally, my willpower is no match for the very real psychological phenomenon called present bias: Our brains light up more when we’re rewarding our current selves than our future selves.

Research has also shown that you imagine your future self almost like a stranger — it’s tougher to care about that stranger than about who you are right now. But that night, I saw near-future-me using that $200 on next summer’s vacation. I wanted the vacation more than the boxes. So I abandoned my cart.

I had managed to use a psychological savings trick: Find a goal that helps you envision your future self. With this epiphany in mind, I asked some of my fellow Nerds to share the savings habits they’ve put to work in their own lives. Perhaps reading these can give late-night you some saving inspiration.

Kimberly Palmer, senior writer and spokesperson: I let nonessential items sit in my online shopping cart for at least 24 hours before buying them. It definitely makes me realize I don't need a lot of them! I also informed my children of this rule, and it has helped cut down on their requests — or at least they know they have to be patient.

Karen Gaudette Brewer, head of content: Fellow let-it-sit-in-the-cart person here. I wait for notifications that something's at least 30% off before I make any moves. Ideally, 40% to 50% off.

Julie Myhre-Nunes, managing editor: When I browse online, I add an item to my shopping cart and wait 24 to 48 hours. After that, I either decide it’s a waste of money/an impulse purchase and delete it from my cart (or forget about the cart altogether), or I decide I want it and make the purchase — it’s the former 99% of the time.

Why it works: “Waiting 1 to 2 days allows me to take the emotion out of purchasing. I no longer succumb to marketing or sales, and instead make spending decisions based on what my family and I actually need or can use.” — Julie again, eloquently making the point for me.

Caitlin Constantine, managing editor: My one real shopping weakness is books, and I’ve found I can get a very close approximation of that feeling without spending an outrageous amount of money by going to the library, wandering around the stacks to see what books might look interesting, and checking out a bunch of them. Even if I don’t end up reading them, I’m still helping the library with circulation numbers, so I see it as a win-win.

Spencer Tierney, senior writer: Plus one to Caitlin Constantine’s “my one real shopping weakness is books.” If I want an older or smaller book, I'll try to find it at one of four libraries I belong to on Libby, the library e-book reader app. (The Libby waitlist for new books can take months, so I have to account for that.)

Why it works: There’s no secret here: It’s nice to get free stuff. You might be surprised what the library has to offer, like movies, magazine subscriptions, games, classes and theater tickets.

Pamela de la Fuente, managing editor: We always tell people to automate savings, and I do in my high-yield savings account, but Dasha Kennedy, the woman behind “The Broke Black Girl”, told Elizabeth Ayoola on the Smart Money podcast that you should invest, even a little bit every week or so, for future you. So I just set up a small recurring deposit to my robo-advisor.

Why it works: You only have to make this decision once for your future self, not over and over again. And if you do it early enough, you could avoid being part of the 41% of Americans who wish they had started investing earlier, according to a 2026 NerdWallet survey.

Athena Cocoves, managing editor: To cut down on food delivery, I started cooking when I feel like it instead of when I’m supposed to. I exercise free will and make soup at 10 p.m. It sounds more obvious than it feels, and it's made a big difference in my budget. And it'd make an even bigger difference if I wasn't also rewarding myself with fancy spices and vinegars, but a girl's gotta splurge somehow.

Ryan Brady, lead writer: My wife takes advantage of a T-Mobile freebie that gives us a discount for DoorDash deliveries. She uses it to buy groceries from Aldi instead of takeout. Aldi is far from us. Publix is right across the street, but more expensive. So this saves us money on the actual items and also helps us not impulse buy (as we often do when we're in-store shopping).

Why it works: You don’t need to call on willpower if you can avoid the situation that tempts you to spend money.

» Read more: Strategies to save on groceries that actually work

Kenley Young, managing editor: I use credit cards for most purchases to get those sweet, sweet rewards, but there's a lot in this article that I've also taken to heart.

I've started using library resources more, and it's saving me money on things like monthly subscriptions.

I've negotiated down several monthly bills, too: refinanced my car loan, got cheaper homeowners insurance, opted for a little less auto coverage in exchange for a lower premium, and haggled online with everyone from Xfinity and SiriusXM to my local newspaper until they all gave me a discount.

Plus, I've opted for some home improvement projects with the expectation that my utility bills would be lower. A plumber finally fixed our toilet, which has led to lower water bills, and I even installed solar panels.

Lastly, my analog skill (playing live music) has become a steady side hustle. I play eight to 10 gigs a month, where (on top of my baseline rate) I also get tips, free food and beer.

Why it works: Because you’re Kenley and you put in a lot of effort.

But you don’t need to be Kenley to find a savings habit that works for your personality, your financial situation and even your musical talents. You just need to experiment. Pick the strategy that speaks to you most, and test it out. Which one are you going to try first?

#3072. Warren Buffett and Greg Abel Just Sent Shockwaves Through Wall Street With This $377 Billion Warning

The time to be fearful when others are greedy has arrived.

This has been a year of immense change for Berkshire Hathaway (BRKA -0.01%)(BRKB -0.25%) and its shareholders. At the end of last year, longtime CEO Warren Buffett, who outperformed the benchmark S&P 500 (^GSPC +0.31%) by more than 6,000,000%, retired. This paved the way for his understudy, Greg Abel, to take over the company's day-to-day operations and the oversight of its $359 billion investment portfolio.

Although the trillion-dollar conglomerate that the Oracle of Omaha built has a new leader, the message, both good and bad, stays the same. While Berkshire's portfolio remains highly concentrated and focused on the long term, Warren Buffett and Greg Abel just sent shockwaves through Wall Street with a $377 billion warning.

Warren Buffett and his successor, Greg Abel, have been net sellers of stocks in 15 of the last 16 quarters. Image source: Getty Images.

Earlier today, Nov. 7, Berkshire Hathaway released its third-quarter operating results, which featured a $12.7 billion operating profit and a significant uptick in share repurchases.

But contained within Berkshire's operating results was a figure that Wall Street and investors can no longer ignore. The company's cash pile, comprised of cash, cash equivalents, and U.S. Treasury bills, ballooned to $377.4 billion.

Berkshire Hathaway is now sitting on a staggering $365 Billion in cash, enough to buy 472 companies in the S&P 500 🚨 🤑 https://t.co/D3tR2PV45p

Usually, a well-funded balance sheet would be viewed favorably by the investing community. But given that Buffett built Berkshire Hathaway into the trillion-dollar company it is today through acquisitions and investments, $377.4 billion sitting in cash and earning interest isn't a welcome sign. Wall Street has become accustomed to seeing Berkshire's bosses put this capital to work.

Furthermore, Berkshire's third-quarter consolidated cash flow statement shows that $426 million more in equity securities were sold than purchased. For the 15th time over the last 16 quarters (four years), Buffett or Abel were net sellers.

While Warren Buffett bent or broke several of his unwritten investing rules over multiple decades, the one rule he and his successor, Greg Abel, refuse to break concerns value. Both are absolute sticklers for getting a good deal, and today's stock market makes finding a bargain incredibly challenging.

In a rare 2001 interview with Fortune magazine, Buffett lifted the lid on his favorite valuation tool, the market-cap-to-GDP ratio, now known affably as the Buffett indicator. He referred to this indicator as "probably the best single measure of where valuations stand at any given moment."

When backtested to December 1970, the Buffett indicator has averaged approximately 89%. This is to say that the total value of U.S. stocks has averaged 89% of U.S. gross domestic product (GDP). In August, the Buffett indicator reached an all-time high of 236.42% and remains well above its historic average.

Stock Market reaches most expensive valuation in history after the Warren Buffett Indicator hits 239%, surpassing the Dot Com Bubble, the Global Financial Crisis, and the 2022 Bear Market 🤯 👀 https://t.co/K5LBAN6S2Q

It's no coincidence that the Oracle of Omaha was a net seller of stocks for 13 consecutive quarters leading up to his retirement, or that Abel has been a net seller in two of three quarters since taking the reins.

History shows that premium valuations aren't sustainable over the long run. While it's impossible to accurately predict when stock market downturns will begin, history has a way of rhyming on Wall Street, at least with regard to outsize valuations.

Suffice it to say, Buffett's and Abel's warning to Wall Street is reaching deafening levels.

TL;DR: Mortgage rates dropped today, but inflation data could shake things up next week.

With the midterm elections behind us, mortgage rates are continuing their gradual slide this month. One factor is a sell-off in tech stocks, which can send investors toward the relative safety of bonds and help push mortgage rates lower.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage ticked down to 6.96% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is five basis points lower than yesterday and 11 basis points lower than a week ago. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.)

Meanwhile, a stronger-than-expected jobs report could slow that slide by reinforcing expectations for another Federal Reserve rate hike in December.

And a reminder: While the economy never sleeps, markets are closed on the weekends. The rates you see Friday are unlikely to change much (if at all) until Monday.

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

The recent slide in mortgage rates might reverse course if next week’s inflation data comes in hot.

This week, the Nerds are watching the October Consumer Price Index, which comes out on Tuesday, Nov. 10. CPI is one of two key measures of inflation, which the Federal Reserve aims to keep in check relative to the strength of the labor market. (The Fed looks more closely at the other data set, the Personal Consumption Expenditures Index, which comes out Nov. 25.)

Right now, the labor market is looking pretty darn healthy: The October jobs report, released today from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, showed U.S. employers added 165,000 jobs in October, far more than economists expected, and unemployment edged down to 4.1%.

Raising the federal funds rate is the Fed’s main tool for bringing inflation down, but rate hikes are only on the table when the labor market is strong enough to handle it. Right now, it’s looking fairly likely that the Fed will approve a rate hike when the committee meets Dec. 8-9. The Fed doesn't set mortgage rates directly, but an anticipated rate hike can put upward pressure on mortgage rates, which respond to investors’ expectations for the economy and Fed policy.

Still, a jump in mortgage rates isn’t a sure thing. October’s inflation data will capture the effect of the Fed’s last rate hike, which came in the middle of September. If that worked as expected and inflation shows signs of slowing, mortgage rates will be less affected.

Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

#3069. AI debt fears ease ahead of Oracle, Alphabet and Amazon updates. Here's what to watch.

Fears over artificial intelligence debt have eased after a bout of volatility. But more tests for AI debt are coming.

Oracle holds its Investor Day on Wednesday. And hyperscalers Alphabet and Amazon.com are scheduled to report quarterly results after the market close on Wednesday and Thursday, respectively.

Credit markets are on edge over a flood of AI debt, though fears have eased up a little lately. Meta Platforms' plans for a $95 billion stock offering, announced on Monday, helped bring down its credit-default swap spreads. Those spreads had risen last week when the company reported negative free cash flow in the third quarter. Other CDS spreads had moved higher too, though they have since backed off.

Investors had expected Meta to bring a large bond deal to market shortly after its earnings announcement, said Richard Cheng, head of Nuveen's investment-grade corporate sector team. The fact that it wasn't announced came as a relief.

"Just the absence of the bond deal itself is a direct catalyst for AI-related spread tightening," he said.

A credit spread is the difference in the yield between the corporate bonds and Treasurys of similar maturities. When spreads tighten, it means investors are becoming more confident about the bond issuer.

The market action over the last few days shows that investors are recognizing that "credit fears may have been overblown," said CNBC contributor Paul Meeks, head of technology research at Freedom Capital Markets.

"I expect that these better feelings, maybe not good but better, may continue as companies announce their quarters over the next few weeks."

Still, spreads on CDS remain wider over the past year due to a surge of debt issuance and free cash flows turning negative across the AI space. Meta's CDS spread, for instance, is still up 177% year to date, while Amazon's spread has gained 129%.

"It's not necessarily fundamentals," said CreditSights analyst Jordan Chalfin. "It's more, I'd say, 80% driven by technicals and sentiment."

Alphabet and Amazon pose the next big hurdle for tech bonds as they update their capex plans and free cash flow forecasts. Microsoft's earnings are also due Wednesday, but the company has yet to issue any bonds to pay for its AI spending.

Both Amazon and Alphabet reported negative free cash flow in the second quarter and analysts expect that trend to continue.

Analysts expect Alphabet to report free cash flow of -$2.3 billion while spending $55.2 billion on capital expenditures in the third quarter, according to FactSet consensus estimates. Amazon is expected to report -$9.9 billion in free cash flow against capex of $58.7 billion.

S&P Global Ratings estimated in an August report that the hyperscalers will have negative free operating cash flow in 2026 and 2027.

More critical will be their outlooks, Cheng says. "The singular focus on the investors' minds is really what the capex guidance trajectory looks like across the hyperscaler space."

Meeks believes elevated capex is a sign of strong AI demand. The hyperscalers have "decided that with all the evidence they have — and they have more than you and me — that this is worthwhile spending, and not just worthwhile; it's required," he said.

CreditSights' Chalfin doesn't expect the hyperscalers to announce major new bond issuance around their earnings reports. Oracle's updates may be more critical for credit markets. The company has issued $117 billion in long-term debt and is clinging to an investment-grade credit rating of BBB-, the lowest level of investment grade above junk, according to S&P.

"It's the most important IG tech credit, just given how it's a bit more stressed relative to the A-rated names," he said. "It's trading more like a high-yield credit, even though it's IG, and so there's just a lot of investor concern on that one."

One wrinkle to the AI debt story: balance sheets don't reveal the whole picture. The companies are using complicated off-balance sheet arrangements for data centers and chip financing, and they aren't fully transparent, S&P Global said in a September report.

"There are commitments they are entering into, for example, into data center leases or purchase commitments on chips that aren't necessarily treated as debt," Mark Habib, digital infrastructure sector lead at S&P Global Ratings, said on CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" Monday.

S&P is trying to provide the market with more visibility on those commitments "to give a fuller picture of what kinds of obligations they're actually entering into," he added.

Oracle aside, hyperscaler credit ratings are all comfortably above A levels — reflecting the fact that they have broadly diversified revenue streams, ample coverage for interest payments, and capacity to add leverage if they choose.

Nuveen's Cheng isn't concerned, pointing out that while there has been some credit repricing, there is no credit crisis.

"They continue to have exceptional credit profiles, strong cash generation liquidity," he said of the largest hyperscalers.

"The market is really not concerned about credit quality at this point," Cheng added. "It's really just the trajectory of the capex needs and the supply of debt to fund that. Both of those are pointing in one direction — and that's up."

Correction: This story has been revised to reflect that Oracle's investment-grade credit rating is BBB-, according to S&P. A previous version mischaracterized the company's credit rating.

#3066. AMD Stock Just Fell Below the Price I Said I'd Pay for It.

The chipmaker's 2027 outlook didn't change on Thursday, yet its stock dropped 17%. How should a buyer get in?

Shares of chipmaker Advanced Micro Devices (AMD +11.04%) lost about 17% of their value in one session on Thursday, Nov. 5, closing at $404.40. The company itself didn't announce anything new that day.

Instead, chip stocks sold off across the board as election wins by candidates who vowed to limit artificial intelligence (AI) data centers fueled rising worries about the AI boom. The Philadelphia semiconductor index fell 12.3%, its worst day since March 2020.

After AMD's third-quarter results on Nov. 3, I wrote that I'd consider buying the stock if it traded around $480. That price was 30 times the non-GAAP (adjusted) earnings per share analysts expect AMD to post in 2027 on average, which is about $16. Thursday's close is around 16% below it.

What changed between Tuesday night and Thursday's close? As far as I can see, just the share price did.

Even after Thursday's fall, AMD stock is up around 89% in 2026. But it's also about 38% off the all-time high close it set on Oct. 6 ($649.42) -- lots of ground to give up in a month.

Meanwhile, the business is speeding up. Showing how much demand there is for its data center chips, AMD's third-quarter revenue rose 45% from a year earlier to a record $13.4 billion. AMD is guiding for around $17 billion in fourth-quarter revenue, about 66% more than in the same period of 2025.

And on the Nov. 3 earnings call, CEO Lisa Su said AMD now expects revenue to rise over 80% in 2027. Put another way, growth is accelerating, from 45% in the third quarter to around 66% in the fourth and more than 80% for 2027 overall.

Might the political worry in Thursday's sell-off hold that back? An analyst asked Su on the call about the land and power behind next year's ramp.

"We have been planning for this ramp with our customers jointly. So we have good visibility into 2027 ... land, power, shell, all of those, the data center infrastructure," Su said.

Simply put, the data centers AMD's chips are going to next year seem mostly planned already. Tighter rules for new construction could matter more for 2028 and later than for 2027.

The $16 estimate is worth checking against AMD's own numbers. In the first nine months of 2026, the company's adjusted earnings per share were $5.12. Management's fourth-quarter guidance for revenue, margins and expenses implies about $2.90 more, for about $8 this year. Reaching $16 would mean a doubling.

Yes, that's a big leap. But AMD is already showing how profits can outpace sales. Adjusted earnings per share climbed 74% year over year in the third quarter, well above the 45% revenue growth. What's more, chief financial officer Jean Hu told analysts that operating expenses for 2027 should grow less than half as fast as revenue.

If revenue grows over 80% and operating expenses grow at under half that rate, I think a doubling of earnings looks reachable.

At Thursday's close, AMD shares sold for around 25 times the 2027 earnings analysts expect, on average. At my $480 buy price, the stock cost 30 times those expected earnings. At the October record, it cost around 40 times expected earnings. Buyers are now paying much less for the same expected profits than they were a month ago.

I'd buy in steps. After all, a stock that fell 17% in a day and about 38% in a month can keep falling, even when the business looks fine. And one of the worries driving Thursday's drop (new limits on data centers) might take months to play out, with headlines along the way pushing chip stocks around.

There's a reason in AMD's numbers, too. Free cash flow was $554 million in the third quarter, down from $1.5 billion a year earlier, as the company added to inventory and spent on capacity ahead of next year's sales. Until cash catches up with earnings, the stock might remain volatile.

My plan would be to buy a first chunk around Thursday's price and add the rest in a few pieces over the coming months -- a simple form of dollar-cost averaging. This way, a further drop would just mean buying the later pieces at a lower price.

In the end, AMD's outlook looks as strong as it did on Nov. 3, and the stock is around 16% below the price I said I'd pay. To me, that's enough reason to start buying. Still, maybe the stock gets even cheaper. So I'd buy it in steps.

#3061. Alphabet's $15 Billion Investment in Malaysia Data Centers Shows That Midterm Results Won't Stop the AI Boom

Fears of midterms slowing down the AI build-out are overblown, much like all things with AI over the past month.

One question has been at the center of artificial intelligence (AI) investors' minds ever since midterm results came out. Will the Democratic Party's gains cause the AI boom to slow down? Shortly after the results were official, Alphabet (GOOG +0.78%) (GOOGL +0.78%) made an announcement that showed AI expansion is far from over.

Google's parent company announced a $15 billion investment in data centers in Malaysia. It demonstrates that tech companies are comfortable with overseas investments if midterm results create more hurdles in the future.

Although investors will be looking closely at how Democratic wins in key states affect the AI build-out, especially in Texas, Alphabet's $15 billion investment isn't exclusively tied to midterm results. The timing of the press release fit right into the news cycle, but it takes a lot of time to plan out these types of deals.

For instance, Alphabet had previously invested $2 billion in Malaysia in 2024, when former President Joe Biden was still in charge. A Democratic president and majority also didn't stop Alphabet from investing $9.5 billion in the U.S. in 2022, with a large portion of that earmarked for data centers.

Alphabet is also still building data centers in the U.S. The company has held this approach for Republican and Democratic majorities. The previous Democratic administration welcomed AI and let its sprawl continue. Biden happily touted one of Microsoft's data centers in Mount Pleasant, Wisconsin, emphasizing that it would create 2,000 new construction jobs. The tone toward data centers sounds a little different now, but data centers are still being built.

International data centers have become more common. Microsoft launched its largest data center in India this year, and India's data center market is projected to maintain a 13.37% compound annual growth rate (CAGR) through 2035. That projection came out months before the midterms.

Some investors may think that international data center construction will grow thanks to the midterm election results. However, that growth was going to take place anyway. AI demand is so intense, and shortages have become such a constraint, that tech executives are discussing setting up data centers in space.

Political uncertainty isn't anything new, especially for tech giants. International data center growth will continue regardless of whether U.S. data center growth accelerates in tandem or slows down.

Substantial amounts of capital flow into this industry every quarter. The tech companies that gave us cloud computing, e-commerce, and other innovations did not stop their march toward progress regardless of which party controlled Washington. That pattern will continue to play out in the AI boom.

#3053. The 1 Investing Habit That Separates Stock Market Millionaires From Everyone Else

Picking great investments is helpful, but it's not everything.

Becoming a millionaire by investing in stocks isn't easy, but with enough time and one habit in particular, on paper it's a very attainable task. Research by Fidelity indicates that there were 769,000 401(k) millionaires at the end of June 2026, who as a group have been investing for an average of 25 years.

Those investors have a range of different backgrounds, money stories, and lives. Yet, unlike many of those who are not yet millionaires, they likely share one investing habit in particular, and probably almost without exception.

People who have made millions investing in stocks have the habit of consistency. Consistency can mean many things, but I'm willing to bet that nearly all of these millionaire investors got a lot of mileage out of consistently investing in an index fund, like the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (VOO +0.30%).

That exchange-traded fund (ETF) tracks the S&P 500 and has an expense ratio of 0.03%. The fund itself launched in 2010, but buying the index was possible long before that. Buying the index is one of the most reliable ways to get a good return on capital over long periods of time. The S&P 500 compounded at a pace of about 10% annually from 1928 through 2025 when dividends were reinvested.

That long-term performance opens up a lot of doors for those with time.

A 25-year-old in their first real job investing $100 per week throughout their career, until age 65, would see that 10% return (on average) play out in their favor again, and again, and again. Their $208,000 in contributions across their working life would ultimately compound to reach a value of roughly $2.4 million. Moreover, building those millions really only required thinking about the investment one time, briefly, at the very start, when the investor set up an automated plan to purchase the ETF once per week.

Despite the minimal thinking required for that investment, investors would, in truth, need another kind of consistency to capture the full benefit: emotional consistency.

The S&P 500, like all markets, goes through bear phases, bull phases, crashes, and episodes of intense trading. Wanting to pause contributions during or right after a crash or a bear market is only human. But that's actually the wrong move. The best approach is to maintain a consistent long-term view, with index fund investments made each week regardless of the market's behavior at any given time.

To let up on the gas right when prices are lower is to let fear get in the way of consistency, and that's something the most successful stock investors avoid if they can.

Index funds aren't the only things worth buying consistently over time. Millionaire investors often consistently purchase certain high-performing blue chip stocks that have reliably stood the test of time.

For example, Costco Wholesale and Apple are the kind of durable and evergreen businesses that could be worth buying every month on a perpetual basis. Both companies have large, loyal customer bases, high brand value, and consistent earnings growth across a variety of economic environments. However, keep in mind that this habit magnifies whatever you aim it at over time. Most stocks are poor targets, as they're not able to adapt to the ever-changing economic conditions in which they operate.

The last reason why consistency is the most important habit shared by millionaire stock investors is that consistently showing up to invest whenever you're able will, over the long run, likely beat those who didn't bother to show up regularly.

Even an investor with an imperfect investing schedule, not much capital, and an imperfect judgment of which assets to buy will likely beat those who invest only when they feel rich enough (and confident enough) to risk money, or only when they're motivated by a flight of fancy. So set a schedule, ideally through automatic contributions to a 401(k) plan, lock in for the long run, and don't give up.

Consistency is a habit that can be built, and for serious investors, it's a must-have.

#3050. Trump's Recent Warning Is Sending Shockwaves Through Wall Street. Here's What It Could Mean for Your Retirement Savings.

The dollar continues to lose purchasing power.

Love him or hate him, President Donald Trump's time in the White House has historically correlated with strong stock market returns. In fact, the benchmark S&P 500 (^GSPC +0.31%) is up by over 39% since his inauguration in late 2024, showcasing widespread optimism among many on Wall Street.

So far, excitement about his pro-business policies has helped investors overlook severe macroeconomic challenges like tariffs, inflation, and unsustainable deficit spending. Let's dig deeper to see how much longer the honeymoon period might last and determine what effect the recent midterm results may have on market performance in the near term.

Like many Republican presidents, Trump has embraced a largely pro-business stance, passing the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which featured tax cuts and deregulation. The administration has also struck a favorable tone toward new energy projects and data center construction, which is especially important for the U.S. tech sector as it embarks on one of its largest infrastructure buildouts in history to support generative AI.

That said, it is increasingly clear that this one industry is helping prop up an otherwise lackluster stock market and (arguably) struggling economy.

According to CME Group, the information technology sector now accounts for a whopping 40% of the S&P 500's market cap. This level of concentration is risky in and of itself. But it is also allowing Wall Street to ignore the growing scale of macroeconomic challenges in the US.

Many of the biggest economic challenges stem from the administration's deliberate policies. These include Trump's tariffs, which have helped bring the average U.S. levy on all imports to around 9.6%, and the war in Iran, which has sent Brent crude prices up 55% since the start of the year.

US inflation now stands at 3.7%, well above the Federal Reserve's 2% target, forcing the central bank to keep rates elevated to control consumer prices. This has also corresponded with soaring Treasury bond yields as investors get nervous about the government's ability to manage its $40 trillion in debt.

Treasury bonds represent the risk-free rate in the economy. And when they rise, they can reduce investor appetite for risky growth stocks while also increasing the cost of capital these businesses need to expand. The Trump administration doesn't have a convincing strategy to fix these issues.

In an October interview with Time Magazine, Trump suggested that higher levels of inflation could help pay down the debt "very rapidly". The logic is that by devaluing U.S. currency, inflation will also devalue the national debt and make it easier to manage. These remarks should be taken as a warning that the administration may be willing to maintain its current inflationary fiscal policies over the coming years.

Inflation is one of the most devastating things for investors and retirement savers because it constantly erodes both savings and financial market returns. Even if you earn the S&P 500's average annual return of 10%, an inflation rate of 3.7% takes your real rate of return to a much less impressive 6.3%. That said, this isn't the time to panic.

Over the long haul, the U.S. has shown a remarkable ability to self-correct and bounce back from crises, and this time probably won't be the exception. The recent midterm results could impose some checks and balances on the Iran war and on some of the government's most extreme spending plans (such as a proposed $1.5 trillion military budget), which could help calm the bond market and bring down inflation.

Yes, the U.S. economic situation remains uncertain, but there may be light at the end of the tunnel. Investors should also focus on diversifying their portfolios across a variety of asset classes to avoid being overly exposed to downside risk in any particular one.

#3049. Anduril Keeps Winning Billion-Dollar Contracts and You Can't Buy It. Here Are 3 Public Stocks That Get Paid Alongside It.

You don't have to buy Anduril stock to get exposure to its long-term growth.

Anduril is trying to disrupt and modernize the technology supply chain for the U.S. military. It recently raised $5 billion at a $61 billion valuation to expand its manufacturing capabilities for drones, underwater vehicles, and other military technologies it is developing.

The problem is that individual investors will find it nearly impossible to buy shares of Anduril because it is privately held. However, Anduril does not manufacture pieces of its technology itself, with many suppliers and partners working alongside it. Here are three stocks that get paid alongside Anduril's growth and could be attractive buys right now.

First up is Kraken Robotics (PNG +0.90%). The small-cap stock sells various components for modern subsea military technologies. These include insulated batteries that operate at great depths, sensors, sonar equipment, and other components used on submarines and underwater drones.

Securing the oceans for commerce is becoming increasingly difficult due to modern drone technology, as evidenced by the current issue in the Strait of Hormuz. Kraken is selling components like batteries and sonar equipment to defense contractors like Anduril, which is manufacturing an underwater drone that can help navies monitor and secure assets without putting humans at risk.

In 2026, Kraken is estimating it will generate over $300 million Canadian dollars in revenue ($212 million U.S.). With its recent large acquisition of the Covelya Group to consolidate its position as a subcontractor in underwater equipment, revenue should grow to much larger levels in 2027. With the stock down to a market cap of $1.1 billion, shares could be a good buy to ride the Anduril wave.

Moving from the ocean to the air, Anduril has a direct partnership with Archer Aviation (ACHR +14.73%) to develop an electric vertical takeoff and landing (eVTOL) aircraft for the U.S military. By leveraging vertical takeoff technology and battery-powered propulsion, Anduril believes it can develop an eVTOL drone for military applications.

Besides an Anduril partnership, Archer Aviation does not have much of a financial business to show for itself today. Revenue is minimal because its commercial eVTOL is still working through approvals from the Federal Aviation Administration, a process that will be quite difficult for a novel aircraft technology. Upfront investments are leading to significant cash burn, with free cash flow of -$681 million over the last 12 months.

This makes Archer Aviation a riskier stock to bet on to ride the Anduril growth wave than Kraken Robotics, which has real revenues today.

Last is Karman Holdings (KRMN +42.13%), a defense subcontractor that sells components that help missiles and rockets maintain structural integrity at intense heat and in harsh operating environments. These components are sold to rocket companies and missile providers.

Anduril is trying to disrupt the legacy missile supply chain amid the increased need for interceptors and will need to work with Karman Holdings to get its manufacturing up and running. The more missiles that Anduril produces, the more orders will flow to Karman Holdings.

The company is also more diversified, with more than one customer. Its revenue grew 24.4% organically to $182.5 million last quarter, with a backlog of $1.3 billion, up 65% year over year. Backlog growth is the key, as it indicates future growth locked in with its various defense and spaceflight customers.

Karman trades at a premium valuation, with a price-to-sales ratio (P/S) of 7. However, this valuation could decline quickly if Karman continues to grow at an aggressive pace.

Depending on your risk tolerance, these are three stocks you can buy to ride any growth of Anduril's business behind the doors of private markets.

#3047. Robinhood shares fall as crypto slump weighs on profits, offsetting gains in new businesses

Robinhood shares were down around 8% in pre-market trading on Wednesday as investors digested weaker-than-expected third-quarter earnings despite growth in options trading and prediction markets.

Here's how the brokerage performed in its quarter ended Sept. 30, compared with Wall Street estimates, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:

Robinhood's net income fell to $468 million, or 51 cents per share, from $556 million, or 61 cents per share, a year ago. Revenue represented a 12% increase from $1.27 billion in the same quarter last year.

Despite that gain, transaction-based revenue of $867 million came in below Wall Street estimates from StreetAccount of $879 million, putting focus on whether Robinhood can sustain momentum across its trading businesses and reduce its reliance on volatile market activity.

Robinhood has been diversifying its business as it tries to expand its brokerage app into a broader financial services platform. Options trading and event contracts have become increasingly important sources of transaction revenue, while the company has continued to invest in wealth management, subscriptions and other offerings.

Transaction-based revenue grew 19% from the same period last year to $867 million, driven primarily by a more than 500% increase in event contracts revenue. Additionally, options revenue grew 31% to $399 million and equities revenue rose 41% to $121 million.

Those gains were partially offset by cryptocurrency revenue, which fell 55% to $120 million.

Chief Financial Officer Shiv Verma told CNBC event contracts on crypto movements did well in the quarter, offering investors another way to express a view on crypto despite the slump in prices and spot trading.

Net deposits on the Robinhood platform totaled $15.7 billion for the quarter, equal to a 17% annualized growth rate based on total platform assets at the end of Q2 2026. Over the past year, net deposits totaled $71 billion, representing 21% growth compared with total platform assets at the end of Q3 2025.

—With reporting from CNBC's Robert Hum and Kate Rooney

#3046. History Says Energy Led All Sectors in the Last Bear Market. Here's What's Different Now.

Energy stocks have delivered exceptional gains in 2026, but a surprising shift in the oil market could change the outlook for investors.

Energy stocks were the clear winners during the 2022 bear market. The S&P 500 energy stocks delivered a total return of 65.7%, while the broader S&P 500 (^GSPC +0.31%) lost 18.1%, including dividends.

Energy stocks are leading again in 2026, but without a broader bear market. S&P 500 energy stocks have gained 42% so far this year, compared with a 12% gain for the broader S&P 500 index, excluding dividends.

In 2022, rising oil prices boosted energy companies' earnings, while inflation and aggressive interest rate hikes weighed on the broader market. The 2026 rally has been supported by oil supply disruptions in the Middle East, with unusually high refining margins. But a recovery in global oil supplies could put pressure on energy profits and stock valuations.

ExxonMobil (XOM +0.34%) reported earnings of $55.7 billion in 2022, compared with $23 billion in 2021. Chevron's (CVX -0.15%) earnings also more than doubled to $35.5 billion in 2022. Both companies returned billions to shareholders through dividends and share repurchases.

However, April 2025 offered a different picture. President Donald Trump's tariff announcements triggered a sharp market sell-off. The S&P 500 fell 21.3% from its February 2025 peak during intraday trading, but did not officially enter a bear market based on closing prices. But S&P 500 energy stocks fell 13.7% in April 2025, making energy the worst-performing sector.

Rising concerns about slowing economic growth and weaker oil demand negatively impacted energy stocks in April 2025. This also demonstrated that energy stocks do not outperform during every market downturn.

The U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) estimated that 4.8 million barrels per day of Middle East crude oil production remained shut down in September 2026, compared with a peak of 10.9 million barrels per day in May. But damaged pipelines and risks to oil tankers continued to affect shipments.

However, EIA expects global liquid-fuels production to fall short of consumption by around 1.3 million barrels per day in 2026. The production is then projected to exceed consumption by approximately 5 million barrels per day in 2027. This represents a potential swing of nearly 6.3 million barrels per day in the global liquid-fuel supply-demand balance.

This forecast assumes that supply routes will reopen and production will also recover. If that happens, rising inventories could reduce oil prices even without a recession in the U.S. The EIA forecasts annual average Brent to decline from $96 per barrel in 2026 to $84 per barrel in 2027. However, renewed geopolitical tensions or slower infrastructure repairs could delay the recovery.

Oil markets are already responding to expectations of easing supply disruptions. Brent crude prices dropped below $100 this week. Hopes of peace agreements involving Iran and Ukraine contributed to the decline, even though the underlying supply disruptions had not been fully resolved.

In the third quarter of 2026, ExxonMobil's Energy Products segment, which includes refining and fuels, reported earnings close to $7.2 billion. Chevron's downstream business earnings also more than quadrupled to $4.9 billion in the third quarter of 2026.

However, these strong downstream earnings may not persist. Disruptions to refineries in the Middle East and Russia have constrained gasoline and diesel supplies. This has pushed their selling prices higher relative to crude oil. However, as damaged refineries resume production and fuel supplies recover, the difference between refined product and crude oil prices could narrow.

Lower crude prices could also hurt earnings from oil production. ExxonMobil estimates that every $1 per barrel change in Brent crude prices would affect its annual upstream after-tax earnings by approximately $700 million, based on expected 2026 operations. Applying this sensitivity to the EIA's projected $12-per-barrel decline in annual average Brent crude oil prices suggests a potential $8.4 billion annual headwind for Exxon's upstream earnings. This estimate assumes that Exxon's production volumes, costs, and other operating conditions remain largely unchanged.

According to FactSet Research Systems' Oct. 30 report, S&P 500 energy stocks traded at 13.2 times expected earnings over the next 12 months, significantly lower than S&P 500's forward 12-month price-to-earnings ratio of 18.7x. However, the valuation of S&P 500 energy stocks was above its own five-year average forward 12-month PE of 12.6.

According to analyst estimates compiled by FactSet, S&P 500 energy sector earnings are expected to decline 7.8% in 2027, compared with projected earnings growth of 16.3% for the broader S&P 500. This suggests that energy's lower valuation relative to the broader market may reflect expectations of weaker future earnings, rather than necessarily making the sector a bargain.

I would avoid aggressively buying energy stocks after their substantial gains in 2026. A recovery in oil supplies could weaken earnings, even if the broader stock market remains strong.

#3037. Colgate-Palmolive vs. Kraft Heinz: With the Market Turmoil, Which Stock Is a Better Buy?

Colgate-Palmolive's steady cash flow stands in sharp contrast to Kraft Heinz's costly portfolio overhaul, and the valuation gap between the two may be wider than you expect.

With the recent market turmoil, investors may start looking more closely at defensive stocks like Colgate-Palmolive (CL -2.16%) and Kraft Heinz (KHC -2.80%).

Colgate-Palmolive dominates personal care categories like toothpaste, while Kraft Heinz focuses on massive scale within the packaged food industry. This comparison breaks down their latest performance and valuation to help you decide which belongs in your portfolio.

Colgate-Palmolive operates a diverse business model focused on oral care, personal care, home care, and pet nutrition. The company sells its products in more than 200 countries, reaching a vast global audience of consumers, dentists, and veterinarians. In its latest annual report, the company noted that Walmart (WMT -1.72%) and its affiliates accounted for approximately 11% of sales. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business.

In FY 2025, revenue reached nearly $20.4 billion, which represented growth of approximately 1.4% compared to the prior year. The company reported net income of roughly $2.1 billion for the period. This resulted in a net margin of nearly 10.5%, indicating a decrease from the approximately 14.4% net margin recorded during the previous fiscal year.

Kraft Heinz is a global food and beverage giant producing items for at-home, restaurant, and on-the-go occasions. As a major player among food stocks, the company operates in multiple countries and relies on a mix of independent brokers and direct sales. In its latest annual report, the company noted that Walmart represented approximately 21% of net sales in FY 2025. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business.

In FY 2025, revenue reached nearly $24.9 billion, a decrease of approximately 3.5% from the previous year. The company reported a net loss of nearly $5.8 billion for the fiscal period. This led to a net margin of roughly -23.4%, which was a significant shift from the positive net margin reported in the prior fiscal year.

Colgate-Palmolive faces risks from its extensive international operations, where foreign currency fluctuations and geopolitical instability can impact financial results. The company competes in an intense global market against private labels and direct-to-consumer brands that challenge its pricing power. Additionally, the company must manage the ongoing financial uncertainty and potential costs related to talc-related litigation.

Kraft Heinz deals with intense competition in the food and beverage industry and the constant need to predict shifting consumer preferences. The company is managing substantial indebtedness and recently announced the divestiture of its North American coffee business, which competes with brands like J. M. Smucker (SJM -2.03%). It also faces potential risks from U.S. tax audit disputes and recent non-cash impairment charges on its intangible assets.

Kraft Heinz appears significantly cheaper based on its lower earnings multiple and sales valuation, while Colgate-Palmolive commands a premium for its consistent profitability and global brand leadership.

From Nov. 2 to Nov. 6, the S&P 500 dropped 3.1%. That's from a mix of factors, ranging from uncertainty around the election to fears of a growing bubble in artificial intelligence stocks to everyone trying to figure out whether December will feature an interest rate hike. With all of that going on, it's no surprise that investors may look to more defensive stocks, such as consumer staples. Each of these companies has a long history of operations, and each pays a dividend. As of this writing, Kraft Heinz's dividend yield is 6.5%, while Colgate-Palmolive's yields 2.2%.

At first glance, Kraft Heinz may look like the better opportunity, given that dividend yield. While Kraft's dividend yield is high, it's also in the midst of a turnaround plan after pausing a split of its business segments. That turnaround is still a work in progress, as the company reported last week that net sales for the third quarter of 2026 declined by 2%. In comparison, Colgate-Palmolive reported that its net sales increased 4.6% in the third quarter.

In addition, going back to that dividend yield comparison, Colgate has an edge over Kraft, even though its dividend yield is lower, because it is a Dividend King. By increasing its dividend payout for 63 consecutive years, it easily met the requirement to become a Dividend King by increasing payouts for at least 50 consecutive years. So while Kraft wins the yield battle, Colgate-Palmolive wins the reliability battle for its dividend payouts, and as of the most recent quarter, its sales are also increasing. That's why, between the two, when adding a defensive position to a portfolio, I would rather own Colgate-Palmolive.

For release at 2:30 p.m. EDT Share

The Federal Reserve Board on Thursday requested public comment on two proposals related to establishing a regulatory framework for Board-supervised payment stablecoin issuers under the GENIUS Act.

The first proposal would require that Board-supervised payment stablecoin issuers fully back their stablecoins with certain permissible reserve assets, such as short-term Treasury bills and certain other high-quality, liquid assets. The proposal would also establish standardized capital requirements to address certain credit and operational risks of payment stablecoin activities, as well as risk management standards, in accordance with the law. Separately, the proposal would introduce rules for Board-supervised firms that safekeep the assets backing payment stablecoins. It would also clarify the permissibility of stablecoin and related activities for Board-supervised banks.

The second proposal would establish a tailored application process for Board-supervised banks applying to issue payment stablecoins. These applicants would be required to submit a business plan and financial information, among other documents. The proposal would also create a process governing appeals, hearings, and final determinations for applications.

The comment period will close 60 days after publication in the Federal Register.

#3028. $6.3 billion Binance hack is largest crypto theft on record

Binance said Friday that a security incident impacted about $6.3 billion in client assets, with around $3 billion frozen on-chain, marking the largest crypto hack on record.

The company later added it began recovering assets impacted by the breach after pledging to cover losses using its Secure Asset Fund for Users, which the company created in 2018 as a protection for clients in the event of a hack.

It wasn't clear how the attack took place. The world's largest crypto exchange initially said the hack may involve "a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, which allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions." However, Co-CEO Richard Teng later said the attack involved a more complex process rather than the misuse of a single engineer's permissions.

The FBI said Friday it was aware of the incident and was in touch with "relevant public and private partners to understand the scope of the activity, evaluate ​potential impacts, ​and ⁠coordinate appropriate investigative steps."

It wasn't clear either who was responsible for the breach. But TRM Labs, a blockchain intelligence and AI investigations company, pointed to North Korean hackers as the potential culprits. "Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists, including the Bybit hack and the KelpDAO hack in April 2026: small Tornado Cash withdrawals funding an operator wallet, staging that began well before the theft, and signatures obtained in advance then executed in one burst," the company said in a post.

Blockchain data platform Chainalysis also said this appears "be the work of North Korean cybercrime group TraderTraitor. This group has repeatedly targeted the cryptocurrency industry, exchanges, DeFi protocols, and investors, to raise funds for the regime. We base our intelligence assessment on on-chain activity observed in the hours following the hack."

Binance temporarily suspended withdrawals while it overhauls its withdrawal security systems and has revoked the affected address authorizations, Teng said. The exchange is also working with law enforcement and blockchain intelligence firms to trace and recover the stolen funds, while deposits remain unaffected.

Binance co-founder Yi He said deposits remained unaffected and continued to operate normally, while the exchange was working on enhancements to its withdrawal service and related address controls. It expects to begin resuming withdrawal services within the next 48 hours.

"We have found no evidence of any wallet private key leak. We will share a detailed technical post-mortem once the investigation is complete and the facts are fully verified," Binance said.

The announcement followed moves by several crypto firms, including Circle Internet Group, Tether and Ripple, to freeze funds tied to the hack.

Exploits are not uncommon in the crypto space. In 2025, Bybit suffered roughly $1.5 billion in losses due to a hack. More recently, Bitget lost more than $350 million worth of digital assets in a cyber theft incident. Over the past several years, bad actors have also drained billions of dollars in crypto from decentralized exchanges.

This week's breach "proves our exact point in proposing regulations for crypto markets earlier this month," Michael Selig, chairman of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, said Friday in a CNBC "Squawk on the Street" interview. The U.S. derivatives regulator on Oct. 5 proposed a framework that would effectively put crypto exchanges under federal government oversight — after Congress failed to approve legislation to regulate the asset.

"The real issue here is that these are unregulated offshore exchanges, and they don't have the same sorts of safeguards that we have in our financial markets here in the United States. We want to offer a federal option to these exchanges to come and register with the CFTC, and they would be subject to the same sorts of cyber security safeguards that we have in our markets today," he said.

Bitcoin fell more than 4% to $77,187.60 on Friday as the hack weighed on crypto markets.

Circle CEO Jeremy Allaire said Thursday evening in a social media post that the company had frozen more than 800 million in USD Coin associated with the incident. USDT stablecoin issuer Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino also said in on X that his firm had frozen more than 1.5 billion of its stablecoin that may have been related to a potential breach.

Jack McDonald, Ripple's senior vice president of stablecoins, said it was actively freezing affected funds held in RLUSD, its U.S. dollar-backed stablecoin.

The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation and the Federal Reserve Board today published feedback letters for resolution plans submitted in October 2025. The agencies did not identify any shortcomings or deficiencies in these resolution plan submissions.

Resolution plans, also known as living wills, describe a banking organization's strategy for orderly resolution in the event of material financial distress or failure. #3020. Federal Reserve Board finalizes changes to enhance the transparency and public accountability of its stress test and reduce volatility in its stress test-related capital requirements

An official website of the United States Government

Review of Monetary Policy Strategy, Tools, and Communications

Mergers, Acquisitions, and Other Applications

Financial Stability Coordination & Actions

Financial Market Utilities & Infrastructures

For release at 9:00 a.m. EDT Share

The Federal Reserve Board on Wednesday finalized changes to enhance the transparency and public accountability of its stress test and reduce volatility in its stress test-related capital requirements. The two final rules are largely similar to the proposed rules from 2025. The Board also requested comment on a proposal to better capture differences in banks' business models to generate fee income.

The Board conducts stress tests to ensure that large banks are sufficiently capitalized and able to lend to households and businesses even in a severe recession. In December 2024, the Board announced it would modify the test to improve its resilience.

"The stress test is an essential component of our regulatory capital framework," said Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle W. Bowman. "Today's changes preserve its resilience by ensuring that it is transparent, granular, and risk-sensitive. The public will now have greater assurance that the risks banks take will be reflected appropriately in their stress test losses and their capital requirements."

The first final rule requires the Board to invite public input annually on the stress test scenarios and any material model changes. It also updates the framework that guides the design of the hypothetical scenarios and adopts the models that will be used for the 2027 stress test. In addition, the final rule makes several adjustments to the stress test calendar. The final rule also updates the global market shock component, which is a set of shocks to specific market components applied to banks with large trading books. These banks will now be tested against two global market shock components each year, and the Board will use the shock that produces the largest losses for each firm to calculate the firm's stress test results.

The second final rule requires the Board, when calculating stress capital buffer requirements, to average the results from the two most recent annual supervisory stress tests for firms subject to the stress test in both years. The Board will begin averaging stress capital buffer requirements in 2028 to ensure that only models incorporating public input are used in the calculation.

The proposal would request public comment on a revision to the Board's noninterest income model that would improve the stress test's ability to capture business model diversity across firms. If adopted, these adjustments would replace the current noninterest income model that projects each bank's fee income under stress. Comments are due 60 days after publication in the Federal Register.

Together, the changes are likely to reduce year-over-year volatility in capital requirements by approximately 50 percent and are not expected to materially affect aggregate capital requirements.

#3015. OpenAI bugging suspect Alfozan pleads not guilty

The Saudi national charged with planting a listening device in the headquarters of OpenAI while he worked there pleaded not guilty on Friday during an appearance in San Francisco federal court.

Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, was sent back to jail after the brief hearing. Alfozan has been held without bail since his arrest on a criminal complaint in early October.

He faces a maximum possible sentence of five years in prison if convicted in the case.

A grand jury indicted Alfozan on Oct. 27 on a single count of interception of oral communications, court records show.

Prosecutors say that he put a recording device in a television in an executive conference room at OpenAI's offices in San Francisco on Sept. 28.

Alfozan's lawyer declined to comment after the hearing before Magistrate Judge Peter Kang.

The judge ordered Alfozan to next appear in court on Nov. 17.

Alfozan is a venture partner in a Saudi Arabian venture capital firm, Raed Ventures.

"He currently serves as Engineering Lead at OpenAI, with a focus on AI Agents and the data platform," Alfozan's bio page on Raed's site says.

Prince Khalid Bin Bader Al Saud, a member of Saudi Arabia's royal family, is a venture partner in the same firm.

Alfozan's case comes as U.S. companies such as OpenAI are making rapid advancements in developing artificial intelligence agents, and as concerns grow about the potential theft of AI tech from those companies.In June, President Donald Trump, in an executive order on AI innovation, said it was U.S. policy "to protect American ingenuity and intellectual property from exploitation and theft by adversaries; and to cultivate America's advanced AI-enabled capabilities."Trump has had a close relationship with Saudi Arabia. But he has also taken steps during his second term in the White House to limit the number of visas for highly skilled foreign workers.OpenAI earlier this year held discussions with Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, the country's sovereign wealth fund, about investing in the company.

— Jordan Novet reported from San Francisco
